Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance 
IMSC: J(1)-MA-1 
By: matcha_tea, edited by: ghastlygrenadine 
Background 
Raid Farms was a server experiment started by YouTuber PineconeLP that described itself as a
“semi-anarchyish[sic] Minecraft server with a unique blend of features,” intending to “…make
Minecraft servers fun again”. The server’s establishment followed a video made by PineconeLP
titled “Why Most Minecraft Servers Are Boring,” which described the need for anarchy and
pvp in order to achieve fun in a server. 
However, since its launch on the 16th of November 2025, players have gradually lost interest
and became bored of the server. On the 1st of March 2026, Raid Farms officially shut down.
[3][5][6] 
Despite its downfall, Raid Farms was a unique and interesting experiment. Through its ups and
downs, its playerbase largely stayed put and anticipated for the next big change. 
This article will focus on how these players bonded, established communities, and seemingly
played against the server’s established intentions. 
 
I. The spawn square 
Most new players’ experience of Raid Farms would be its spawn area – the 100 by 100 metre
square that serves as the centre of the server, houses shop and studio apartment plots, and has
a quaint lake where players can fish. The square also has PvP protection and is the only area in
the entire world where griefing is banned, which explains why immediately outside the square
massive, towering cobblestone structures loom over you. 
 
Although, despite the initial unsettling feeling that the griefing brings, these structures actually
provide valuable nostalgia and realism to the server, reinforcing the sense of community early
on in a new player’s experience. Each skyscraper tells a story of history, previous player
interactions, and a once lively community that made a boring wilderness have a sense of
character, even if it is unsightly.
title: Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance

content:
16 
 
An infamous griefer was Zeke, who has a celebrity-like status within the server. He has a
presence in the form of signs around the whole world, signed with “griefed by zeke”.
Zekethegameboy. [8] 
 
II. The tunnel 
 
Notice the cobblestone, dirt, and other planks dotted around on the seafloor. Players try to adapt
to traverse the tricky terrain, but the many breaks in between show they usually resort to other
ways of travel (e.g. on top of the mangrove trees). 
I came across a tunnel running outside the Raid Farm’s spawn square that ran under a
waterlogged swamp, eventually emerging into the outskirts of a savannah. 
The diagonal passageway reminded me of foot tunnels under rumbly tube tracks in London,
loosely put together, filthy everywhere, and littered with masses of cigarette butts and random
splashes of paint. The imperfectness of this tunnel describes Raid Farms as a server very well.
It embodies the spirit of anarchy in all its forms – carelessness, disorder, and chaos. 
In servers where griefing is permitted and has no restrictions, the time and effort required to
build a building will always be greater than the effort required to destroy it with TNT. The
ragtag-like presentation and composition of the tunnel is a result of players understanding this
fact. The result is a randomly, carelessly repaired, unmanaged tunnel. I will refer to this
phenomenon as the Griefing Imbalance. 
In a server where griefing is banned, plots are enabled, and almost all players do not want to
grief, a nicer looking tunnel made of planks, logs, and lit with lanterns may have been built.
Helpful signs along the way would guide players to their destinations. 
However, in Raid Farms, such a construction would be an extremely large risk. A griefer could
easily destroy the tunnel that took hours, even days to build, in seconds. The large structures
title: Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance

content:
17 
around spawn also amplify to naive new players that such efforts are welcomed, but also warns
that it is likely to be short-lived. 
You may conclude because of this that Raid Farms is a disconnected, unfriendly community
due to its hostile architecture. Nevertheless, like Cialazar, a town I will talk about in the next
section, the message that is associated with the unpolished tunnel is what makes the server have
an unseen community. It communicates the resistance and resilience of players in the server
despite its circumstances. So, in fact, the Raid Farms community is stronger than any other. 
 
III. Cialazar 
 
To the four cardinal directions around the square, there are many bridges made from cheap,
easy-to-find materials running in parallel with each other, seemingly leading nowhere. This is
the first of many examples in Raid Farms where the consequences of its anarchic nature are
displayed through the structure’s composition. 
 
At the end of one of these bridges, you are greeted with a sign showing the city’s name –
Cialazar – apparently named after its founder, Ciala, according to Ob1cloney1234. [2] 
Looking in the Discord server again, the first mention of it seems to be by someone named
Pudd in the #general chat. Similarly, the same player with the tag PuddPuddofMaja was also
the first to say the city’s name in the Minecraft chat, pointing another player to its very own
Discord server, on the 18th of November 2025. [7] 
This is just one small part of the very fascinating lore and story of this specific town, and of
course there are numerous more dotted around the world. The abandoned ghost city is also
referred to as Ctown, which is most likely a portmanteau of Cialazar and town.
title: Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance

content:
18 
 
Inside the city’s walls, there were unmanaged stalks of bamboo reaching up to twenty or thirty
blocks tall, evident of the city’s age and its history. The unmanaged, wild, overgrown bamboo
made me feel like I was wading through unmanaged fields in the English countryside, with
bees, mosquitoes, and flies all swarming around me as I explored around. The mildly griefed
ground also mimicked that unmanaged countryside look; the imperfection and ruggedness gave
the city character and tells its once vibrant story. 
 
Another observation I made was the buried chests around the city – a cheap and efficient way
that players used to protect their items from raiders and griefers. 
These kinds of chests are a direct result of anarchic server design with unrestricted griefing and
PvP, forcing less equipped players to have to hide from other players to survive. This is in direct
contrast to one of Raid Farm’s main goals – to foster communities and player interaction. [3] 
Furthermore, this is also another example of the Griefing Imbalance, where the effort put into
mining, farming, and collecting resources must be hidden away to prevent hostile actors
destroying that progress. Players, who ultimately act as people, need a common space, physical
or otherwise, to bond and form relationships. However, Raid Farms punished establishments
and institutions that represented communities, people, and societies through the imbalance,
which furthered the distance between players. 
Although, Ctown is the perfect microcosm for Raid Farms, where community exists at the same
time as seclusion and scepticism. The server was systematically structured to be an anarchy
server, but the players inhabit it as if it was an SMP server. The balance in between is the
amalgamation that produces this small settlement. Although this article does not intend to
discuss why the server failed, I believe that even though Raid Farm’s intentions as a server
mixing the best of both worlds was successful, neither world’s players enjoyed the final product.
title: Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance

content:
19 
IV. The Diner 
 
This building had a restaurant/diner on the bottom, with hotel rooms or some kind of flats
above. 
In a spread out, disconnected server, the more signs a place has, the more people visited it, and
found a sense of comfort and belonging, leading them to place a sign to mark their presence in
the very rare communal spaces around the map. The “X was here” signs allow players to not
just be a random person, a meaningless entity in the server, but is the only way (in Raid Farm’s
anarchic server) for its members to share a moment – and most importantly, a space. 
I talked about this in my recent video [1] where I explain the effects and mechanisms of healthy
and harmful interactions, however it is also worth pointing out the indirect interactions a
server’s environment can provide and act upon a player. 
Servers have a direct, symbiotic relationship with players, where players influence the
environment, and the environment influences the players’ decisions; this means that anything
placed in the environment is directly interpreted by bystanders as influential to them, especially
so if the structure was made by a player – in Raid Farms, these influential structures are signs. 
 
V. The Compound 
 
The last structure I went to was called The Compound – a small, rectangular, cobblestone
structure, with a wheat farm in the middle. There are some chests and barrels dotted around the
farm too for storing wheat seeds, but they are all scavenged empty. 
The wheat farm being at The Compound’s very centre shows how a server’s mechanisms
influences player behaviour greatly. If it was not for wheat’s “value” as a currency (even though
it failed, and players did not like it), the people who built this rudimentary building introducing
new players would not have a wheat farm as its welcome. This speaks to the actual consequence
and effect of the wheat currency, which is as a social glue. In a server that has no real, effective
mechanism to draw players into a central, communal area, something else must shape their
identity.
title: Raid Farms: A symbol of resistance

content:
20 
You might even be able to draw comparisons between minority diaspora communities with
Raid Farms players – groups of people who cannot interact or share experiences together due
to some kind of systemic oppression or force, and must use discrete, shared, community spaces
where they can interact without outside intervention attempting to pull them apart. Truthfully,
the cohesion that Raid Farms players have and showed when Pinecone announced the server’s
closure was evident – they were never enemies or hostile to each other, but the system in which
they live in created the environment where they are not able to interact freely with each other,
and even if they were, it was not something that Raid Farms actively encouraged. 
 
Conclusion 
De jure anarchy servers with a de facto SMP playerbase (survival Minecraft players who want
to interact with other players and share builds) will always create a stark divide between the
system’s expected outcome and the players’ inherent assumed outcomes on that server. Raid
Farms’ mechanisms allowed its landscape to be griefed, which caused players to spread out
because of that fact. However, players have always secretly been yearning for interactions, for
community, for someone to play with, and this was evident by the masses of screenshots people
shared on Raid Farms’ Discord server for everyone to reminisce on the systemic oppression of
the people’s will for community.

Fun, wins, and losses 
IMSC: J(1)-MK-1 
By: MrMillerPink, edited by: koviubi 
Introduction 
In activities of any kind, a type of win and loss will be present. Whether it is finishing your
build in a building game, having it be destroyed, or finding loot in adventures. However, you
may not recognize that winning can be a broad term applicable in many contexts, and the same
can be said for losses. Both have their own consequences towards players. Thus, when
designing Minecraft servers, one must be especially familiar with the topic so crucial to fun. 
This article provides more clarification on fun, winning, and losing in videogames, highlighting
key information I’ve learned throughout studying game design. 
 
 
I. What is fun? 
What I’ve noticed during my time in the Institute of Minecraft Studies (IMS) Discord server,
is the rather arbitrary understanding most people have of fun. Fun is not exclusive to a specific
activity like socialization, player interaction, rivalry, or teamwork! There are many ways to
have fun and players prefer different activities. Therefore, excluding other activities by entirely
dedicating our research to a few would be delinquent. 
 
We need a definition of fun for this article to even exist. I’ll be using Gabe Newell’s “ad hoc
definition” of fun which he stated in an interview.[1] Gabe Newell is the CEO of Valve, an
American video game developer, publisher, hardware, and digital distribution company. He is
a competent game designer and was involved in the making of the corporation’s earliest games.
He and his team defined fun as “the degrees to which the game recognizes and responds to the
players’ choices and actions”.
title: Fun, wins, and losses

content:
5 
 
This definition is the best one I know. Some degree of time and effort is put into every choice
the player makes: be it walking, breaking blocks, fighting monsters, etc. It’s really important
for game designers to reward players for their efforts, as it’s the basis for fun to take place.
Players want to feel that their choices and work have meaning and impact to the world around
them, so we should make their impact apparent. 
 
II. Wins and losses 
It’s easier to explain wins by analyzing the ones in Minecraft. When you build a makeshift
shelter on your first night, win a pillager raid, or even kill a single spider, that’s a win! Wins
come in different sizes and forms, and people seek out and enjoy different types of activities. 
However, wins can feel empty if we don’t give them impact or reward. When you fight and
loot trial chambers, it’s satisfying because you made the decision to fight, you beat the
challenges, and dealt with the risk of losing your items; when you finally beat it, you get a
reward! In this situation, the player had agency, information was properly communicated, and
most players felt fairly compensated by the end of it. 
It’s a fundamental skill in game design to reward and show a player's work. Too little or no
reward will make activities feel pointless, and if it’s mandatory, it’ll feel like doing chores. Too
much could make a reward not feel earned or desensitize the player's feeling of reward. 
However, getting swiftly blown up by a falling creeper, getting pestered by phantoms, or
accidentally throwing your items into lava also feels frustrating. Why? Even if it technically
was the player’s fault, they were given no awareness or agency, and they were punished by
something they didn’t do or did unintentionally. This feels unfair! 
Players should be able to tell why they lost, at least in hindsight, and they should absolutely be
given ways to deal with their issues. Minecraft isn’t a great example of this as the game has
issues of being too soft or just annoying; so another game must be used as an example.
title: Fun, wins, and losses

content:
6 
III. An example of fair wins and losses 
Risk of Rain 2 is a roguelike fighting game with a unique mechanic: the more time a player
spends the stronger the enemies become. To avoid the enemies becoming far stronger than the
player, said player must perform a balancing act of collecting and purchasing loot around the
stage by killing enemies to gain coins, while also progressing through the game by getting to
the next stage to collect and buy more loot. 
Taking too long to get more powerful or excessively searching a singular stage for the last
chests/items has led to the death of many. However, players can leave any time they want
(though they’ll have to defeat a boss to earn their progression). This, alongside the many other
measures the game has to help it feel fairer, has made Risk of Rain 2 feel surprisingly fair,
especially for a game in the roguelike genre, which is home to a lot of randomization outside
the player’s control. 
The enemies are also very well designed. They often appear in large crowds, yet somehow you
have a good understanding of what’s happening around you when you fight. Information is
adequately communicated to players, and that will help make deaths feel fairer and a result of
their own incompetence rather than a fault of the game. 
That fairness combined with the reward of getting incredibly strong items as a result of your
skill and smart decisions, and seeing enemies you once struggled with get defeated easily make
Risk of Rain 2 a very enjoyable experience. 
Although it’s a game that strays far from Minecraft’s gameplay, the ways it approached its
gameplay are exemplary when viewed in its whole. 
 
IV. The cost of competitive multiplayer 
Another example is Fortnite. Competitive games with multiplayer can be very fun if done right!
The loss feels real and it’s a true test of your skill and decision making that comes with
satisfying victories. It may also create interaction with others in the form of rivalries that
amplify satisfaction, and also through strong teamwork that strengthens the connection
between people. 
However, there is a hidden cost inherent to it. In a competitive multiplayer environment, there
has to be a loser. In a game of Fortnite, one player has to be 100th place, which feels
embarrassing. Half of the players won’t make it to the top 50. Only one player or group can be
1st. Losing sucks! People need to win more than they lose to have fun, but in Fortnite, there
will always be a loser. The people behind the game made bots to counteract this, and it came
with understandable backlash from the community.[2] Competitive multiplayer is expected to
be exactly that: competitive and multiplayer. Adding bots to where players expect real people
disrupts the premise and promise of fighting other humans, not a machine. 
The playstyle that was advertised and supported in Raid Farms were alliances and rivalries, but
that meant the destruction of one group in favor of another. This is yet another issue of Raid
Farms and anarchy in general, the core gameplay involves discouraging players from
continuing to play. In anarchy Minecraft servers, there is an expectation of hostility among the
title: Fun, wins, and losses

content:
7 
players in the form of fighting or griefing. However, these activities that come at the cost of
another player’s enjoyment. There was an infamous incident of corruption in Raid Farms
involving a normal player encountering Pinekitten, a person close to Pinecone, the YouTuber
and owner of Raid Farms. The player attempted to kill her, but she was saved by intervention
from Pinecone. Afterwards, the player was banned. 
This event is clear proof that Pinecone has faced the issue inherent to competitive multiplayer:
enjoyment deriving from another person’s loss. He resorted to intervening with cheats to
resolve it, which led to the person who attempted to kill Pinekitten, and perhaps even more, to
leave.

Game design is the core of making games, as it’s the method and adequacy of which a game is
made in order to achieve its goals. That is why I believe that more game design discussions are
needed in the MSTI, as it’s being disregarded – even though studying it will improve our

Although you may think I’m against competitive multiplayer, I’m not! Competitions can make

Social Priming and Server Well-Being 
IMSC: J(1)-ML-1 
By: Moldypizzar0ll, edited by: Rev and retrooper 
I. Introduction. 
There is a strong intuition, if not strong empirical evidence, that preexisting concepts,
relationships, and moral obligations play a substantive role in governing the interactions of
players in virtual worlds. I will argue that, at least in the case of Minecraft servers specifically,
conceptual and social cohesion in the real world prior to its instantiation in Minecraft is, on the
whole, detrimental to the life of a server. This is likely due to the fact that such a cohesion
presupposes shared utility functions among the constitutive members of a cohesive group,
which, when augmented by the fact that Minecraft’s gameplay loops allow the player to obtain
an extreme abundance of resources beyond an initial curve, leads to the prioritization of the
individual cohesive unit rather than the server as a whole. 
 
II. Terminological Clarifications. 
A. Priming 
A primed player is a player with preexisting concepts, moral obligations, and rational norms
that bear relevantly on their behavior in-game. To some extent, all players are primed, although
some may be more relevantly primed than others. For example, X may be said to have, pro
tanto, a greater degree of priming than Y given that X has had experience playing sandbox-type
games before, while Y has had no such experience. 
B. Social Priming 
A socially primed player is a primed player whose set of conceptual elements includes
preexisting real-world social relationships. However, these relations must have certain
necessary and sufficient conditions; for it is not sufficient to stipulate that any preexisting social
relationship is a sufficient condition for social priming. Let S be a set1 of players X, Y, and Z.
Insofar as all players in the set are necessarily: 
i) Acquainted with each other and/or share a certain degree of friendship (in 
the ordinary sense of the term),2 
ii) Cooperate with each other more often than not, ceteris paribus, and 
iii) Share similar goals, aims, and moral values more often than not, ceteris 
paribus, 
1 I will assume for simplicity’s sake that a relevant set for us contains three or more players. 
2 By “ordinary” I simply mean the common-sense, non-technical sense of the word.
title: Social Priming and Server Well-Being

content:
25 
then X, Y, and Z can be said to be socially primed with respect to S. From hereon I will assume
that any given socially primed player meets conditions (i)-(iii) and is primed with respect to a
set of players. 
 
C. Utility Functions 
A utility function3 is a function that takes states of affairs of the world as inputs and utility as
its output. Utility is often conceived of in terms of utils. A util is an arbitrary unit used to posit
the utility of a state of affairs or action. Consider two possible actions, A1 and A2, such that A1
produces five utils and A2 produces two utils. On standard utilitarian views, A1 is the morally
obligatory action to take, for it results in a greater amount of utility than A2. Hence, the utility
function of an agent, or in our case, a player, measures the utility generated by certain states of
affairs relative to an individual. Therefore, it is possible for individual utility functions to differ
across agents/players. Consider two agents, P and Q, with utility functions u(P) and u(Q),
where u(x) can be said to be the general form of a utility function. Under u(P), the number of
utils gained by eating ice cream may amount to ten; under u(Q), the number of utils gained by
doing the same thing may only amount to one. Moreover, certain states of affairs or actions
may not even figure into agents’ utility functions at all. This will come into play later. 
 
III. Server Goals and Player Properties 
A. The Purpose of a Server 
It is generally assumed, if not a widely held intuition, that the purpose of a server is to maximize
the amount of enjoyment for the greatest number of players.4 Though this broadly utilitarian
characterization is by no means the only sort of characterization that could be made here, it will
prove useful in setting a fixed point around which the parts of the server may revolve (players,
moderation, gameplay, etc.). The gameplay loops of Minecraft, within the context of a server,
are often used to coordinate the behavioral patterns of players around certain determinate goals
or ends. These goals or ends, by extension, generally serve to increase the extent to which
players may enjoy themselves on the server. Because these ends are only valuable insofar as
players cooperate with others in order to satisfy those ends, we may be in a position to claim
that players include interactions with other players squarely within the domain of their utility
functions. Furthermore, those players would assign positive values to the relevant outputs of
those functions. Let the cumulative utility of all shared events that involve player-to-player
interaction be the Server Utility (SU). 
The central claim here (C) is that: 
(C) All things being equal, i.e., under ideal conditions, servers with players who are socially
primed, viz., with preexisting social, conceptual, and moral relationships with others in the
3 See [2] 
4 Note that this does not necessarily include moderators/staff, or administrators. On this view, if they 
benefit in any capacity, they only do so contingently (I doubt, from my experience, that they enjoy any 
part of it). This may obviously be argued against, but for our purposes here I will take the well-being 
of the players specifically as the primary object of study.
title: Social Priming and Server Well-Being

content:
26 
relevant ways, will always have a lower SU than servers with players who are not socially
primed. 
If this claim is true, social priming is, on the whole, undesirable for a server. If this claim is to
be proven, we must explore the utility functions of socially primed players. 
B. Priority 
Recall the set S of players X, Y, and Z, where each player is socially primed with respect to S.
Assume additionally that each player in the set has a utility function. Because of conditions (i)-
(iii) for social priming, it would be quite difficult to argue that X, Y, and Z do not consider their
fellow players within their utility functions; for if it were to be the case that X could either help
Y or another random player, say A, X will in the majority of cases gain more utility by helping
Y rather than A; furthermore, Y benefits from having X help them when needed. The dependence
relation is thus symmetrical. Let us formulate the first derived claim (D1), or the PRIORITY5
premise thus: 
(D1) For any group of players socially primed with respect to a set, the utility functions of each
of the players within the set take priority6 over the utility functions of any other player, barring
exceptional circumstances (e.g. when there are only strangers present on the server for a given
time). 
The crucial thing to note here is that priming entails PRIORITY; as a player, it is in my best
interests to prioritize my preexisting friends and social relationships over those that I hardly
have any acquaintance with. Hence, I will prioritize the well-being of my friends over the well-
being of the rest of the server. 
This, however, is not enough to prove (C) on its own. It is a trivial observation that I tend to
prioritize people I already know over people that I do not know (yet); but this does not entail,
logically nor probabilistically, that this is harmful to the server overall. I can include both the
general well-being of the server and the well-being of my compatriots within my utility
function. This, however, need not always be the case in situations where social priming is
involved. 
C. First Steps to Exclusion 
Though priority is one way in which a utility function can bear a relation to other utility
functions, in that I prioritize certain agents’ functions over others, there is a second way in
which a utility function can have a relation (or lack thereof) to other functions, that being
exclusion. Let us state the first exclusion premise (E) thus: 
(E) X excludes a utility function u(x) from their own, u(X), when none of the outputs of u(x)
figure into the inputs of u(X). 
However, as of yet, we do not have a reason to think that socially primed players exclude the
utility functions of other server members in any substantive way. At this point, though, we may

philosophy. See [1] 
6 I use priority in lowercase to indicate the concept, while I use PRIORITY in capital letters to indicate the claim
itself. This also goes with further concepts and premises found later.

offer a probabilistic argument for why priority leads to exclusion. This argument is predicated
on the properties of the feedback loops in Minecraft itself. 
D. Scarcity and Exclusion 
In the real world, resources are scarce; economic theory attempts to cope with this fact by
determining the optimal course of action given the constraints on what we can choose.
Minecraft, however, is devoid of scarcity altogether. The game has a theoretically infinite
number of resources (if not a functionally unlimited amount); the only barrier is technological,
or skill based. You cannot access certain resources given that you do not have the means to
acquire them, such as farms, equipment, enchantments, etc.; but given that you do have those
means, the number of resources available for you to collect is functionally indefinite.7 
This means that any given player is entirely self-sufficient; if they so wish, they need not depend
on other players in any capacity, for they are not bound by scarcity in the same way real-world
agents are so bound. The crucial move here is to observe that this feature applies equally well
to groups of players. If a group of players decides to become self-sufficient, as they cannot be
said to be hampered by any sort of real scarcity, they certainly can do so with no effect on other
players in the server in question. Hence, any calculations or rational assumptions regarding the
management of resources, the well-being of the players within the group, or the overall
experience of the group on the server need not factor in, to any extent, the utility functions of
other players or groups of players. In this case, first exclusion (E) obtains. A subsidiary move
here we must make is that a set of socially primed players with prior utility functions is the
most apt kind of group to exhibit first exclusion; for, being primed already with preexisting
utility functions, the probability of their becoming self-sufficient without any dependency
whatsoever on other players is quite high. Therefore, let us consolidate these claims into our
second derived claim (D2), or the exclusion premise: 
(D2) i) X excludes a utility function u(x) from their own, u(X), when none of the outputs of u(x)
figure into the inputs of u(X). ii) A set of socially primed players with prior utility functions is
the most apt kind of group to exhibit (i) pertaining to the rest of the server. 
 
IV. The Full Argument. 
It is evident that if (D2) obtains, then a server with socially primed players will usually always
have a lower SU than servers without socially primed players. For if (D2) in fact obtains, the
set of socially primed players with respect to that set excludes others’ utility functions from
their own evaluations, and hence server-wide events or other server-wide utility-maximizing
forces are excluded from the evaluative purview of the socially primed set. Let us put together
the overarching argument as follows, assuming ideal conditions, e.g. that there are other players,
that these players are not socially primed, that all the utility functions work regularly, etc.: 
Premise 1. There is a set of players S such that the players are socially primed with respect to
S. 
7 This, of course, excludes edge cases in which there are indeed scarce resources, e.g. dragon eggs; but 
the point here is that most resources in the game that matter are functionally infinite, and available to 
anyone with the requisite means and determination.
title: Social Priming and Server Well-Being

content:
28 
Premise 2. (PRIORITY) If there is a group of players socially primed with respect to a set,
then the utility functions of each of the players within the set take priority over the utility
functions of any other player, barring exceptional circumstances. 
Intermediate Conclusion 1. Each of the utility functions of the players in S take priority. 
Premise 3. (exclusion) i) X excludes a utility function u(x) from their own, u(X), when none
of the outputs of u(x) figure into the inputs of u(X). 
ii) A set of socially primed players with prior utility functions is the most apt kind of group to
exhibit (i) pertaining to the rest of the server. 
Intermediate Conclusion 2. S is of the sort that is most likely to exhibit exclusion. 
Intermediate Conclusion 3. So, S exhibits exclusion by probability. 
Premise 4. If a server has a set of players that exhibits exclusion, the SU of that server will on
the whole be lower than a server without such a set. 
Conclusion. (C) All things being equal, i.e., under ideal conditions, servers with players who
are socially primed, viz., with preexisting social, conceptual, and moral relationships with
others in the relevant ways, will always have a lower SU than servers with players who are not
socially primed. 
 
V. Potential Solutions and Conclusion. 
This conclusion accords well with observation; often, preexisting cliques and groups are
scarcely willing to participate in the activities of a server as a whole and prefer to keep to
themselves and their own sphere of action. This is often to the detriment of the server, as such
behavior limits player-to-player interaction, dulls the social life of the server, and renders the
server down to a platform on which individual groups can play on a server without fear of
having to interact with anyone else. 
All the while, this sort of behavior occurs under perfectly rational (in a sense) conditions; it is
through no fault of the socially primed player’s own that they prefer to help or cooperate with
those whom they trust rather than random people on the server. This is simply how we value
others’ actions relative to those we interact with more often. This does not touch, however, on
the moral obligations people have towards others on a server, which may well entail that they
interact with strangers for the sake of the well-being of all and the server at large, a position
that I myself find quite plausible. There is also the problem of intra-server cohesion, which
makes manifest the possibility that priority and exclusion obtain even in groups formed within
the server rather than socially-primed players. If this so happens to be the case, which it
certainly is given that people often form friendships and social groups on the server itself, what
is their ontological and ethical status? Should the server administration curtail their formation,
or deal with their consequences as they go along? What to do about this phenomenon, though,
is not within the scope of this article. 
The most obvious solution, assuming that socially primed players will always be present to
some extent, is to integrate more elegantly the incentives of the server with the incentives that
the socially primed player feels compelled to act on with respect to the set in which they are
title: Social Priming and Server Well-Being

content:
29 
primed. A server may restrict resources and create a sense of scarcity in order that groups are
forced to cooperate and interact. A server may also enforce proximity requirements, requiring
all players to stay within a certain area so as to promote cooperation and shared ends. Another
potential route is the elimination of socially primed players altogether; if everyone were to lack
social priming, there may be more of an incentive on the part of each individual player to
foment social interactions for their continued enjoyment. I, personally, have no opinions on the
matter, apart from generally accepting the conclusion that unregulated social priming is, overall,
detrimental; I leave it up as an exercise to the reader to determine what sort of solution in this
situation, given the foregoing assumptions, maximizes the well-being of a server.

[2] Steele, Katie, and H. Orri Stefánsson, Decision Theory, The Stanford Encyclopedia of
Philosophy (Fall 2025 Edition), Edward N. Zalta & Uri Nodelman (eds.)

Fun in multiplayer environments 
IMSC: J(1)-RV-1 
By: Rev, edited by: MrMillerPink 
Introduction 
Recently, MrMillerPink published his article “Fun, Wins, and Losses” [1] referring to game
design as an optimization tool that should be used in the MSTI. This brief article is, then, my
way of following his advice and adding a second block of reflection on this point. 
I had thought of conveying this as a comment, but I didn't want it to get lost among the many
things that happen in comments; it seemed better, then, to have it published as an article where
I could expand a bit more. 
Thus, this article aims to point out certain limits that appear when using “game design” in
multiplayer spaces, not because they are errors in themselves, but to narrow down the scope of
this implication. 
 
I. What is fun? 
MrMillerPink cited Gabe Newell, to explain that fun is “The degrees to which the game
recognizes and responds to the players choices and actions”. [1] 
I find this definition very satisfactory and self-conclusive. 
And yet, it seems to me that it appeared in a context that cannot be 100% transferred to server
theories. Newell and his team were in the process of designing individual games, where their
design encompasses: the environment's reaction, the physical reaction of movement, the
reaction to the player's actions, the reactions of the player's enemies... etc. 
This problem persists even when MrMillerPink uses the game Fortnite due to a difference I
consider key. Minecraft servers, unlike other multiplayer games, do not base their fun and
interaction on the design of the game per se, but rather reside in strategic forms of interacting
where one cannot have prior information about what other players will do. 
In plain English, this means that unlike games like Rainworld (2017), Risk of Rain 2 has a
predetermined reaction model: Each entity operates under discrete states (Idle, Chase, Attack).
Transitions occur only when specific conditions are met, such as “line of sight” or player
proximity. [2] 
This does not happen on Minecraft servers. Although this pattern of behaviors can be analyzed
in the design of the game itself (as MrMillerPink himself does). The “medium” is different; a
Minecraft server involves (or seeks to involve) other players whose reactions cannot be
designed a priori as they can in a traditional video game. 
This, I believe, means that the “fun” Newell talks about, and by extension what MrMillerPink
talks about, is not the only one at play when applied to a strategic multiplayer environment. [1]
title: Fun in multiplayer environments

content:
11 
On the other hand, this responds to a distinction; a “pre-determined and farmable” recognition
reaction is not the same as an interdependent recognition reaction subject to uncertainty. 
This means that “Miller's fun” taken to its logical conclusion would lead players, after certain
interactions, to learn what is fun in a given game and what is not. This also happens in Minecraft.
The phenomenon of farms is basically the logical conclusion of learning the “mechanics” of
the loops. Likewise, the automation of interactions with the game occurs because in Minecraft
the recognition reaction is pre-determined, farmable, and repeatable under the same conditions. 
In contrast, on a server, part of what attracts players and the fun they derive from what I call
social fun: the fact of interacting with others. It may be in competitive contexts
(winning/losing), but also in broader social contexts where an interaction leads to a reaction,
but since both can meet again, that reaction has meaning beyond the initial fun and builds a
“profile of meaning.” 
Basically, repetition in interactions changes what is fun on a server. After all, you can't farm
PvPs, friendships, connections, or economic systems. 
Let's think of a player who builds an impressive farm. In Miller's framework, the game
recognizes their action (the farm works). But if no one visits it, if no one comments, if no one
integrates it into the server's narrative, does it really feel fun? Technical recognition exists, but
social recognition does not. And it is the latter that builds community. 
With this in mind, I believe this definition must be expanded for a server: 
“Fun is the degrees to which the player feels that their actions and choices in the physical game
are recognized and valued by the social world in a sustained manner over time.” 
This change may seem small, but it is ultimately key. That there exists for the player a “profile
of meaning” and that they have one for others as well. 
For this, I refer not to my intuition, but to that of MrMillerPink himself in his previous article
“A Talk About Anarchy”: [3] 
“One of the greatest joys you can experience in life, is to be observed in a positive light by
someone interested in you, whether it be family, friend or significant other; Not just in the sense
of the core parts of your identity, but also the small things: habits, hobbies, and all the things
you care about. It’s a shame that such validation, admiration and respect is sparse throughout
society. You haven’t lived till someone likes the way you express yourself”. 
This leads me to suggest that the greater the recognition and/or reactions a player's action
produces in a social environment, the greater their satisfaction and “fun” within it. No one likes
to be ignored. 
This is the problem with “Miller's Fun” and my new proposal. And yet, there are still things I
would like to cover.
title: Fun in multiplayer environments

content:
12 
II. The problem of uncertainty 
Robert Axelrod in The Evolution of Cooperation (1984) [4] raised the problem of uncertainty,
one that caused cooperative environments to fail and led to certain failures in maximizing the
interests of those involved, paradoxically due to the belief that their interests were at risk.
Paraphrasing Axelrod, the problem is as follows: 
“The inability of actors to predict with certainty the intentions, behaviors, and reactions of their
counterparts. This informational gap generates a risk of unilateral defection, where the fear of
being exploited by the other (behavioral uncertainty) or ignorance about the duration of the
relationship (temporal uncertainty) blocks collective action, turning cooperation into a
dilemma of failed coordination unless there are signalling or reciprocity mechanisms that
stabilize expectations.” 
This is useful when talking about servers because the presence of “others” with their own
agency and desires that we do not know leads to the uncertainty raised by Axelrod. We fear
that others do not share our interests or that they do not want to interact/react to what we do in
a “public” space, and as previously stated, it cannot be predicted. Likewise, we cannot take for
granted, force, or predict that people will interact with us, or that they will do so positively. 
When I apply this to Minecraft environments, I adhere to what MrMillerPink already
mentioned. [3] 
“My explanation of why the environment of Anarchy servers come about as such is that even
if most players in the server don’t desire hostile interactions with one-another, the players who
act chaos and destruction create incentives for players to not make efforts to socialize, and
instead be suspicious of others whilst also acting viciously to protect themselves. This further
alienates players who desire and make efforts towards amity, causing them to leave, making
the dominant playerbase to consist of those who contribute to this antisocialness.” 
What MrMillerPinker means here is that antisocial behavior is not the majority; instead, in
most cases, it is simply the “most rational” action or the one that “makes the most sense” given
an environment that favors it. In this sense, Axelrod's problem of uncertainty and the chain of
events towards the antisocial that MrMillerPink proposes converge in what Shepsle and
Weingast (1987) [5] called “Structure-induced equilibrium.” 
That is, “in contexts of high strategic uncertainty, institutions act as incentive structures that
alter the utility matrix of agents. The equilibrium is not just the result of individual or group
preferences, but a product of the social environment which, by imposing restrictions and
sanctions, reduces the possibilities of others' behavior, making them predictable and allowing
actors to coordinate their actions under a cost-benefit structure stabilized by the norm itself.”
[5] 
If this is true (and MrMillerPink seems to recognize that it is), then both the uncertainty and
the decision chain of other actors constitute the “Environment” or “structure” that provides
incentives or sanctions for players' actions. In an environment where one does not know what
reaction actions cause, nor which players are “good or bad,” the individual player or group tend
to move away as it is the action that best protects their own interests in the face of high
uncertainty.
title: Fun in multiplayer environments

content:
13 
This is why, for example, players on servers tend to move away from each other even when
resources for survival are present in abundance. 
This phenomenon occurs even more on servers of an anarchic nature, as we would expect if
what MrMillerPink proposes is true. [3] 
 
III. Minecraft and Fortnite 
This problem in general also serves to differentiate interaction and fun in Minecraft and Fortnite.
In the latter, players literally fall from the sky on a bus with their expectations clear; there are
100 players and only one can be alive. There is no uncertainty about what others want to do,
there are no “other things” to do in the meantime; the storm closes the available space,
incentivizing movement towards the center. The structure induces an equilibrium where the
dominant action is to kill each other. 
There may be small variations: if there is a very good player, some might target them in a
temporary alliance. But as MrMillerPink [1] said in his latest article, people like to win, they
like (even more) the reward for winning. Fortnite's structure therefore demands that any
alliance be unstable, short, conditional, and purely utilitarian. Moreover, it is most likely that
99.9% of Fortnite players will never meet or never meet in a truly meaningful way, which
makes it easier to betray, lie, deceive, flee, or target. If it were different and players had to play
together again for a few matches, for example, then we would expect to see fewer of these
individualistic behaviors because acting that way would be frowned upon and could even lead
to being targeted, which would take away the fun. 
In contrast, a Minecraft server is already in a different structural state; fun does not derive from
purely individual achievements (surviving, doing things to progress, etc.). It is also founded on
good coexistence, on fun, meaningful interactions/reactions (as we saw in the previous chapter).
Likewise, Minecraft's design allows, beyond physical limitations, freedom to shape the
opportunity structure on a server. Minecraft does not have “one objective”; there are perhaps
incentives to beat the game and progress materially, but beyond that, it does not have Fortnite's
structure of “you kill or you lose.” This allows for the existence of anarchic servers, where the
structure leads to antisocial behaviors [3], but also a great variety of servers that can propose
an explicit objective like Fortnite, or that can set rules to avoid outcomes they don't like. 
This leads me to one of the solutions (or rather considerations) from Shepsle and Weingast's
(1987) [5] theory, who considered that in their model, institutions not only limit available
options but also act as mechanisms for reducing strategic uncertainty by stabilizing
expectations and shaping the cost-benefit structure for rational actors. For our purpose:
Institutions are Rules, customs, and social norms. 
These considerations lead me to think that what MrMillerPink called “game design” could be
adapted to a Minecraft server as “institutional design” because it is the rules that shape what
players do or do not do, and allow for the “design” of reactions and recognition that respond to
the player's decisions and actions.
title: Fun in multiplayer environments

content:
14 
Conclusion 
In the end, all of this points to a discomfort worth holding onto. Game design gives us powerful
tools, but when we transfer them to multiplayer servers, something resists. We cannot program
one player's reaction to another, neither farm friendships nor automate respect. 
And yet, what we cannot program is precisely what matters most. 
Fun on a server is not just that the game responds to our actions. It's that someone else sees
them, remembers them, values them. It's that awkward and wonderful moment when a stranger
comments on your build, or when your name appears in a conversation you weren't expecting.
It is, as Miller himself said before, being observed by someone who cares about how you
express yourself. 
The problem is that this kind of recognition cannot be directly designed. You can only design
the conditions for it to occur. This is, rules that make others' behavior predictable, spaces that
invite interaction, institutions that punish betrayal and reward trust. Institutional design
prepares the soil for community to decide to grow. 
And yet, uncertainty will always remain; The uncertainty about whether the other will
cooperate or betray. The uncertainty about whether our actions will be recognized or ignored.
This uncertainty is what I consider a condition of possibility. Because if we could predict
everything, if every interaction were guaranteed, then recognition would lose its value. It would
be like just another farm: efficient, predictable, and empty. 
Perhaps that's why the servers that last are not always the most “Game immersed” or even the
best to play on. The servers that last the most are those where, despite the uncertainty, people
keep choosing to form a connection.

[2] Hopoo Games, 2019, How moving from 2D to 3D shaped the design of Risk of Rain 2,
https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/how-moving-from-2d-to-3d-shaped-the-design-of-i-
risk-of-rain-2-i- 
[3] MrMillerPink, 2026, A Talk About Anarchy, Institute of Minecraft Studies 
[4] Axelrod, R., 1984, The Evolution of Cooperation 
[5] Shepsle, K. A., & Weingast, B. R., 1987, The Institutional Foundations of Committee
Power, The American Political Science Journal

The Five Motivations 
IMSC: J(1)-SA-1 
By: Snorka, edited by: matcha_tea 
Introduction 
As server owners and server theorists, our goal is to maximize fun, but that is a nebulous goal
with many disparate ways to accomplish it. This article’s aim is to classify the different reasons
people have fun on Minecraft servers so future theories can focus on maximizing certain
motivations rather than just aiming for the subjective target of “fun.” 
There are the five motivations: accomplishment, creativity, discovery, connection, and
domination. Each of them is present in everyone, just to different degrees. Of course, players
also have their own preferences within these categories and separate from them (e.g. someone
might prefer building in a modern style or a fantasy one, but both fit within the creativity
motivation), but any time you are having fun on a server, it does fit into one or more of the
motivations. 
 
I. Accomplishment 
This is perhaps the broadest category. Players may feel accomplishment after completing
something difficult – the main challenge with adding accomplishment to a server is weighing
difficulty so you add accomplishment without making the game frustrating. The kind of
challenge players must overcome can come in many forms: combat challenges obviously come
to mind, but building farms and other redstone machines is another common thing players do
to feel accomplished. The first three motivations can all be achieved in singleplayer, but
accomplishment is often even better when you can show off what you have done to your
servermates. When optimizing for accomplishment, make sure that players’ accomplishments
can benefit others! 
 
II. Creativity 
A big chunk of Minecraft players are builders first and foremost. Creativity is the motivation
that explains that. Again, the main reason to build on a server instead of a solo world is so other
people can see what you built, so make sure that is possible. When optimizing for creativity,
you want to make most desirable building materials easy to obtain. Although you can get
accomplishment from building with netherite or beacons, that is no more creatively stimulating
than building with cheaper stuff. Another way that accomplishment can look like creativity is
when building is mechanically useful. Making effective fortifications or prisons is an
accomplishment, decorating them is creativity. Keep that in mind!
title: The Five Motivations

content:
23 
III. Discovery 
People like seeing new things. All the structures and biomes to explore in vanilla contribute to
the experience of someone who cares a lot about discovery, but there is only so much to see
there. On a server, ignoring any mods that add more things to see, players can experience
discovery by traveling and coming across what other players have built. To optimize for
discovery, make sure that is possible! If griefing is allowed, builders need to hide their builds,
which harms the discovery experience. Also, concentrating builds in certain areas can make
them easier to find. There’s also a less obvious element of discovering game mechanics (again,
this is largely through mods for regular server players) and social dynamics. You can absolutely
get a sense of discovery through observing a server’s economy, politics, and wars. 
 
IV. Connection 
This is the first of the server-exclusive motivations. People like spending time with their
friends! When optimizing for connection, make sure it is easy to meet up with friends (such as
with tp commands) and to make new ones (this could be a whole theory in itself). Another
aspect of connection is that people like working together with a group, even if the group are
not all close friends. Pre-established or naturally arising factions are great for this, as well as
any content that is only possible (or much easier) by doing in a group. Domination: This
motivation is all about feeling superior to other people. This can come from winning in
competitions, like PvP or minigames, and it can also come from being in charge of a group or
faction. Including ranks is great for domination-motivated players. This is absolutely one of
the more dangerous motivations to optimize for, though. For one person to win, other people
have to lose, and many discouraging moments when you get killed or griefed come from other
players chasing domination. But it is still a major way people have fun, especially in online
games.
title: The Five Motivations

Abstract
Agency and Stewardship theories can be used to describe how we understand the relation-
ship between delegates and delegators, both in the corporate world, in volunteer spaces,
and in The Systems Event. We can understand how the lack of a clear framework, com-
pounding issues from the organization of the event, and player siloing worked against the
desired goals of the event. This essay draws on first-hand experiences and accounts from
related essays, tracing how two competing teams diverged and were impacted during the
events Exploration and Exploitation time frame, largely from the Ordonian perspective.
“The Ordonian Calculus” is posed as a phenomenological analysis of social and systemic
risks and anticipations, and their effects on team cohesion.
The essay also proposes an Agency Theory of Minecraft, arguing that the default
singleplayer design leaves multiplayer environments particularly exposed to agentic, ex-
ploitative play absent of deliberate design intervention, and offers guidance for future
IMS events.

should be adopted as a framework for understanding the social underpinnings of servers,
especially in regard to leadership due to the similarities between server event planning
and a business.
1.2
The setup
According to early promotional materials for the event, it is described as a team-based
event where players are individually tasked with designing a system: “A repeatable struc-
ture of Rules, Incentives, or infrastructure.” These systems would need to fit one or more
of the categories listed: Economic, Government, Society, Infrastructure, Incentive, Indus-
try, or Defense. Players had roughly three weeks through the month of June to submit
a systems draft of their idea for the event, with late comers given a grace period.
In Rev’s article on the Systems Experiment, he describes the event in two phases:
“Exploration” and “Exploitation”. (Rev, 2026) The promotional material calls this Ex-
ploration phase the ‘preseason’. This work will continue using Rev’s reference.
During the event’s Exploration phase, players were free to ask questions about how
the event would be run. These questions were primarily answered by Turtle, the creator
of TSE. One of the questions from ‘Dinosawrr’ (dino.sawrr), as paraphrased by Turtle,
asked, “can outside, non-systems players join as citizens?” (Turtle, 2026a) Turtle’s re-
sponse gives us some insight into his thought process as an event organizer, stating, “no,
people cannot join without following the normal requirements and expectations”. (Turtle,
2026a) He goes on to explain:
While it sounds fine in theory, this will introduce a lot of members who
want to focus specifically on SMP style play. They are likely to get annoyed
with systems over time and bypass them. In addition, we want systems to use
each other (i.e., industry system player sells goods to infrastructure player
with a currency from an economic system player), which might be diluted by
non systems players.
I believe it is entirely possible to design the systems you want without
non systems players, and I think we should think about it more like a cross
between Hermitcraft and Ish civ than just a civ. You people will have more
time than the average team, you will be closer, and you will design systems
that are more intricate. Besides, Minecraft is, as we have seen, a very easy
game for single/low player counts. (Turtle, 2026a)
This shows that Turtle had some foresight into the problems that The Systems Event
could, and in fact, did run into.
From a first glance, it’s clear that Turtle and the
organizers at the IMS wanted this event to produce a certain kind of outcome. The
Systems ‘not an experiment’ Experiment was created to develop and showcase emergent
systems. These systems would be developed competitively by two teams, Alpha and Beta
(Beta would later be renamed to Ordonia).
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
5
Two examples were loosely cited as inspiration for this event.
Civilization Event
servers, with a clear factional focus, large and equally distributed player base, and ses-
sioned play. The IMS, should they choose something like this, must consider these re-
quirements in advance of team formation. These kinds of events are well known to many
in the IMS, with members who have watched or participated in these kinds of events.
The second example was Hermitcraft. It may not be realistic for the IMS to host
events that resemble Hermitcraft per se, but there could be an organizational philosophy
based on that model, except for a structure suitable for our experiments and events.
This assumes that stewardship is valued over agentic gameplay,[a] meaning that robust
systems, narratives, and shared lore are created with each member potentially being a
force-multiplier for each other. In a server, this might mean looser teams, districts, and
less focus on ‘social victories’. This doesn’t mean an end to team-based competitions
entirely, but it could be of a smaller scope inside another event, department, or SMP.
The setup was meant to be in a fairly ‘archaic’ or ‘vanilla’ environment, without much
attention to balanced gameplay with the exception of the banning of End Crystals and
Elytras. (Turtle, 2026b,c) There were few mods on the server, but we did use Simple
Voice Chat and a ‘Wiretap’ mod that provided a speaker and receiver. There was also a
mod for copper rails; however, it did not have a large effect on gameplay, and its presence
went largely unnoticed, only being used by Team Alpha between their settlement and
their ice boat path to the shared neutral mushroom island.
Turtle had found a seed that at a first glance seemed to be perfect for this event.
Team Alpha was given the seed a day earlier to pick between the northern or southern
continent – an advantage that the organizers gave as a concession due to Alpha’s difficulty
recruiting and keeping active members up to that point.
Alpha picked the northern
continent, which had the only Pale Garden biome and the only ancient city that was
found. Ordonia was given the southern continent, which had the largest Badlands and
Mangrove Swamp Biomes. Ordonia’s location would prove useful later for the Nether,
being right next to a Fortress and being the closest to the only Bastion we would get in
this event.
1.3
Good intentions, flawed design
We had a month to draft our systems and work with our teams to refine and plan their
implementation. This ‘exploration phase’ was quite generous on time, with the hopes
that enough people would have drafted and refined the systems they would use in the
exploitation phase. A ‘near-vanilla’ experience, with few guidelines or restrictions beyond
the siloing[b] was intended to allow more emergent systems to be developed.
[a]Gameplay that optimizes for maximal utility of its systems as permitted by the game itself or playing
as if crossing off a checklist. “Given the opportunity, players will optimize the fun out of a game.” A
player engaged in Agentic Gameplay defaults to Exploitation of known-optimal strategies towards a
model of complete-ness, often over the game’s fuller possibility space. This mirrors the Agents pursuit
of individual utility over the Principal or collective’s broader interests.
[b]Sorting of players into teams, often for competitive or antagonistic purposes. Encouraging agentic
playstyles and rationale for the benefit of teams. (Factions, Nations, Clans, etc.)

content:
6
Siloing the player base into teams is a common approach in competitive PvP events;
however, those team are usually balanced in number, large enough to support the lo-
gistical needs of the team, players understand the focus of the event before they go in,
and the victory conditions are often congruent with this scheme. This mismatch in focus
on top of the ‘vanilla’ or ‘archaic’ framing of the event produced a bifurcation of focus
among a small and uneven player base.
We can see how choices in the design and execution of The Server Experiment cumu-
latively might have led to the ending previously described. In “The Consequences of Poor
Design” by Harlow, one of the fundamental issues posed was the lack of clear communi-
cation which led to uncertainty and burnout among sections of the player base. (Harlow,
2026) The problem of poor communication is not the sole or original critical flaw of the
event, but it had several down-stream effects. We should ask: why was communication
here poor?
The Systems Event was meant to develop systems that are the most broadly appli-
cable or replicable inside of many types of servers; when we think of ‘vanilla’, ‘archaic’,
or ‘anarchic’ types of environments, where little gets in the way of player agency, we
are mostly adapting to the structural systems given to us by Mojang. The event also
created structural particularities that detracted from its focus. Given its siloed team-
based nature and the a priori creation of levels of secrecy, the experiment became less
about the face-value goals and more of an impromptu analysis of leadership and player
sociology. By implying formal barriers, TSE organization made a choice that produced
civ-like narratives over Hermitcraft-like emergent collaborative systems.
Hermitcraft is a model for a server of systems-creators in an otherwise mostly vanilla
environment (data and resource packs aside). Each new member has been vetted after
being known by their members for a while. A series might last between one to two years.
An emergent system might take anywhere from a weekend to several months. The key
difference is that hermits are not usually siloed. Each hermit is in some respects a force
multiplier for each other.
1.4
Through a lens of Agency and Stewardship
In the world of business and finance, there is Agent theory and Stewardship theory.
Agency, the more dominant theory, defines formal collaborative relationships between
Principals[a] and Agents.[b] The Principals delegate to Agents. It is in the best interests
of Principals to create control schemes to minimize their risk of mismatched interests
between parties. This poses a prisoner’s dilemma between Principal and Agent, where
cooperation is put up against individualistic utility maximization. This is in contrast to
Stewardship models, which attempts to refute the pessimistic, control-oriented Agency
[a]In business, the Principal is the shareholders who appoint executives as managers of a busi-
ness/organization. In TSE, both the organizing body and the teams act as Principals over the players.
[b]a utility-maximizing subordinate in a business relationship
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
7
framework. Instead, ‘agent’ gets re-framed as ‘manager’.[a] Psychologists and sociologists
criticize Agency Theory[b] as having an incomplete understanding of organizational life
and motivations. So, the question is: What causes interests to be aligned? (Davis, 1997)
The corporate-legal environment, of course, is very different from the Institute of
Minecraft Studies or the Systems Experiment. Unlike a shareholder-executive relation-
ship, no capital or legal obligations bind Principals and Agents. What I am offering
by borrowing this frame is a method of analysis of server or event life. What Steward-
ship and Agency describe here is the uncertainty of the motives of both delegates and
delegators, and how that uncertainty shapes anticipation and control-seeking behavior.
This uncertainty exists whether the currency is dividends or the credibility of systems.
Furthermore, you could extend the corporate examples to something closer to our world.
Volunteer or open-source governance more broadly shows Agency and Stewardship the-
ories into non-contractual settings; the IMS already does this through implementing a
shared mission and democratic modes of leadership in departments. Understanding these
relationships within servers and the IMS broadly could help us understand what is needed
to shape and reinforce the intrinsic motivation that we rely on.
This, of course, brings us back to the IMS and the event. The IMS is a decentralized
organization of volunteers and collaborators. Turtle and the IMS are the originating
Principal from which a stewardship-oriented culture has naturally arrived. This Principal
relationship also comes as a form of what Rev (2026) calls “homophily”.
While Turtle’s response to Dinosawrr’s question was eventually overturned due to a
lack of active players near the July 1st launch of the server (Exploitation Phase), we can
establish the cultural practice of Stewardship are, stated or not, within the focus of this
event, particularly with its relationship to the IMS. Seetloveletter, a member of the IMS
Discord server who has extensive experience with Civ-style events and SMPs, stated as
such that the typical IMS member would not be representative of the typical Civ event
roster. (seetite, 2026)
Despite Turtle’s criticism of ‘Content SMPs’ or ‘Scripted SMPs’ – noting that the
events and player archetypes are made to appeal to a consumer outside of said SMPs –
it is still the case with events that the agents or managers could be described as serving
two principals, and a calculus of sorts had arrived to bridge the gaps where there were
mismatched goals and understandings. (Turtle, 2026, nd)
1.5
Formative consequences
Scorvon: “Ordaina [sic] had a whole city built, banks schools etc, one week
later they were bombed and everything was destoryed [sic];” “you cant win
if ur systems are gone”. (scorevon, 2026a,b)
[a]In business, the individual(s) entrusted to execute the Principals objectives. May behave either as
a self-serving Agent, or collective serving steward, depending on situational and psychological factors.
In Minecraft, a player is a manager of oneself and the environment.
[b]In business, control schemes must be used to reduce the risks posed by conflicting interests between
Principals and Agents.

blAze_floW: “And your victory will be empty if we never finish our systems
in the first place” (blazeflow, 2026)
Scorvon: “[a] win’s a win” (scorevon, 2026c)
A lack of proper communication and foresight given towards the principles of this
event caused a conflict of interest in how participants saw the purpose of the event. For
some, it was meant to be a sportsmanly development of systems, or a casual laboratory
under the eyes of the shared Principal of the IMS. For others, the most obvious approach
was more of a binary.
This split likely formed because of the differences in how the teams form through the
course of the exploration and early exploitation phases. Ordonia had the full extent of
time and the active support of early members of the presidium, particularly with Pheelix
and Blaze. We had two large systems meant to encompass Ordonian life well before the
server actually opened, meant to be the all-stars of the competition. We believed we
were well prepared and advantaged during a time when Alpha was seen, as Turtle put
it, ‘The Resistance’.
This framing seemed to hold even as membership requirements loosened to drive
recruitment. I invited a friend of mine to the event; through which either by neglect or
the organizers’ providence, was assigned to Team Alpha. Ordonia had a spy in Alpha’s
ranks!
Alpha, on the other hand, rose through likely because their conditions favored a
different approach. Their leadership was more centralized under a figurehead like Scorvon
than later Phantom_Boi, but their society was considerably less centralized. There were
no democratic presidium or secretaries appointed via assembly as Pheelix had in mind
for Ordonia.
Where Ordonia was waiting for a city design suitable enough, orderly enough, aes-
thetically harmonic enough, or complete enough in its design – Alpha’s decentralized
approach benefited their city. They had detailed builds, bases, social spaces like a tea
party garden and a colosseum. Ordonia had a collection of cabin-like builds among farms;
an industrial district posing as a town, supporting 4 players hoping that somehow new
life would be put into the server by some manner, while we deliberated systems that were
dreamt up before the server opened.
Alpha’s approach came with some drawbacks though. There were complaints about
the casual and careless use of wind charges, the death of all but one armadillo in an XP
farm that was built out in the open. To us, there seemed to be a lack of cohesion among
members of Alpha. A couple members confided that they were considering building away
from their town. There was a similar sentiment in Ordonia before any headway was made
on the city.
While Ordonia was building up its industry, Alpha crossed off a lot of the usual
accomplishments before finishing the colosseum. They exhausted the trial chambers on

except for the day of the Nether expansion and the Ender Dragon fight.
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
9
1.6
Formation of a calculus
There were signs at the server launch that The Systems Experiment had started off wrong.
There wasn’t much of an official launch. Some Ordonians weren’t even aware when it
launched. We were set into spectator mode to explore a map in which unbeknownst to
us had a smaller world border than we had planned for, until we were able to convince
Turtle to open the map up to its full intended extent. Later, most of the Ordonians
that would be active were set to survival mode on the correct side of the map, but Team
Alpha would continue to face issues with being in spectator or adventure mode until the
next day. Some even spawned or respawned suffocating underground.
1.6.1
A matter of principals
Naturally, Team Alpha was quite upset about this. Ordonians took a stewardship ap-
proach out of concern that the event couldn’t survive without two active teams. We
gathered food, iron, blocks, and saplings from our collection to help them, then sailed to
a small dock they called the embassy. It didn’t take them long to recover. Their team
quickly grew to a size of around six to eight active members compared to our core four,
one of which was unable to participate for the second week. Some of us questioned if
giving them the care package was a wise idea, stating that it removed from them a lot
of necessary work and travel to get some of those supplies, and at our own expense. We
were able to help them ‘cross things off a checklist’. Thus, we can see a conflict between
two instincts and two principals emerge. Do we do what seems best for the event, or do
we serve only the interests of our team? This is the first part of the Ordonian Calculus.[a]
This point is also echoed in Harlow’s ‘The Consequences of Poor Design’, where it
was noted that the typical Minecraft player, one that is not from the IMS, would be
more concerned with getting ahead rather than the “idealistic purism” of “a niche online
community, [like the IMS]”. (Harlow, 2026) It can also be seen how the divergence in
development over time alongside homophily within the IMS led to diverging subtextual
readings about the bounds and priorities of the event.
Ordonia has had a longer, more thorough period of exploration, even while both
teams had the same time window. Ordonia grew during the exploration phase, causing
Pheelix to take leadership much more seriously to handle the increasing player base. One
that did not materialize as expected during the exploitation phase. We also had members
that were active in the IMS broadly, one of which would eventually take the reins of the
systems experiment from Turtle later on.
Alpha benefited from a rush of recruitment and a relaxation of requirements to partic-
ipate in the event after a serious lag in recruitment and activity for most of the exploration
phase. They had less formal ground to work with and some of their active members ap-
plied a different subtext to the event, one that would otherwise serve them in a typical
factions-based SMP.
[a]Social and systemic anticipation during The Systems Event by the individual members. Risk and
failure model assessments unique to members of Ordonia.
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
10
To lay out the principals, the primary principal is the IMS which includes the orga-
nizers of TSE. The other Principal is whichever team the player is on. These principals
would presumptively work against each other because of what was left to subtext. Or-
donia’s core four were in a high demand, low information environment with its members
sharing more responsibility and losing interest.
Alpha didn’t carry the weight of planning or fulfilling large systems in quite the same
sense.
The way that Alpha formed by the opening of the server led to a team that
was primarily focusing on the most legible aspects of the event, with the formal focuses
typically left to whoever was the leader at the time.
The differences in styles of leadership would prove consequential in the way members
– stakeholders in their respective teams – related to power and team organization. Power
and Legitimacy was established with roles and elections during the exploration phase in
Ordonia. Alpha held an election quite some time after the opening of the server. Alpha
did not perceive a need for formal elected roles beyond the sole leadership.
1.6.2
Diplomacy
Scorvon is a player whose history and perspectives were sadly missing from Revs ‘Who
Decides?’ paper. His role as the leader of Team Alpha was as iconic as the power struggle
between him and Phantom_Boi, who eventually beat him in Alpha’s election. He was
a ‘strongman’ of sorts, and an extremely effective leader who saw Alpha’s swift early
progression.
A member of Ordonia intercepted a written book on the mushroom island pertaining
to Scorvon’s leadership and the talks of war. The journal states that war was likely
to take place for ‘entertainment value’. They were aware of the mismatched team size,
and the presence of fully geared PvPers on their team. They wanted to declare when
all Ordonians were active. This would conflict with statements from both Scorvon and
Phantom_boi that the majority of team Alpha did not want war. The journal confirms
this later by stating that many in team Alpha were skeptical about Scorvon, leading to
Phantom_Bois’ victory. In Revs’ interviews, Rev was led to believe that there were no
power struggles in Alpha, and Scorvon was not mentioned in the manuscript as of this
moment. (Rev, 2026)
We became more deliberate in our interactions with Team Alpha, and observed pat-
terns in the way they organized, kept the condition of their town, and tended to coor-
dinate in small sub-groups or as individuals. There were complaints from Alphas that
critical pieces of information, such as the state of treaties, weren’t communicated well
or at all. There was confusion about whether the majority of Team Alpha wanted war
or wanted to avoid war. The most active members were looking for war and often con-
ducted espionage even after we’ve come to agreements about what we expect before
anyone comes to the opposite team’s land. The easiest ‘catch’ was when they required
assistance getting out of our blocked Nether portals, a measure we took after one of us
was killed in the Nether.
However, it wasn’t always quite hostile, thanks to Hilo’s efforts with the Tea Parties
and her work on the mushroom island. There were also trade arrangements as Alpha
