content:
11
was in need of a lot of building materials, and they had the only Pale Garden biome on
the map. In order to get the few resin clumps they had, we needed to be transparent
in why we wanted resin. The biggest point of the resin trade for Ordonia was to gather
information. We were ‘anti-monopoly’, and this incident would give us clues into how
Alpha operates. Resin and its related products had its uses, but was never critically
important. Nonetheless it was a monopoly and a somewhat strategic one. The early-
game question was what their behavior would be towards more strategic monopolies –
like the nether expansion granting either team access to the Netherite Upgrade Template.
Despite the trades and agreements, trust was still uneasy. While individuals within
team Alpha had their own reputation, we were still cautious dealing with any member
of Team Alpha.
We would make sure that Ordonia wasn’t deprived of the template
by creating a rail line hidden low in the nether, covered to be less conspicuous where
it crossed rivers and lakes of lava. We suspected a couple of their members killed an
Ordonian they assumed had the template, but it was in an ender-chest.
1.7
Agentic gameplay
Perhaps the instinct to dominate or grief isn’t incidental to this setting, but rather is
invited by it. Minecraft is primarily built as a singleplayer game. While it can be played
multiplayer, it does not have its own mechanisms built into itself that meaningfully alter
the gameplay or add reasons or mechanisms to compete or cooperate with others. The
systems that vanilla Minecraft provides are maximally legible and exploitable. It is easy
for any experienced player to reach the end game. Minecraft isn’t alone in this though.
For example, Paradox grand strategy games in singleplayer modes are often built to
reward accumulation and expansion, to ‘paint the map’ is rewarded until your game
becomes too boring or tedious to manage. Multiplayer lobbies often ban a list of metas
or strategies. Expansion becomes negotiated among neighbors, and exploitation of your
resources becomes the meta for multiplayer lobbies.
Players move from a utilitarian
and agentic style of play to one more oriented towards stewardship both internally and
externally. This environment is still competitive, but it remains one bounded by rules
and negotiations to the benefit of everyone in the lobby.
These kinds of multiplayer strategy sessions also invite not just a different set of
extrinsic goals, but invite intrinsic ones as well. You’re responding to a different envi-
ronment that doesn’t exist in singleplayer, your choices are going to be different, more
intrinsic to what is happening between players than the meta of the game itself.
Minecraft is built differently because it does not structurally create channels of strate-
gic behavior, yet all the same it is a singleplayer game, with a simple and appealing pro-
gression chain. Build a base, get diamonds, maybe villagers, go to the Nether, then beat
the dragon. It is a binary checklist of things you either did or did not do, and to some
that is part of the point of the game. The game doesn’t prioritize taking a creative route,
navigating roadblocks, sticking by your own principles, or anything beyond the binary
checklist in any structural manner. It is a mostly blank slate devoid of expectations, and
most players will be accustomed to this. This is Agentic Gameplay.
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
12
1.7.1
The exceptions
Hermitcraft is one example of a model of stewardship, even when storylines reflect agency
or rivalries for part or whole of a series. Pranksters and Institutions like the Permit
Office offer some antagonism to varying degrees; however, it is all within the bounded
context that Hermitcraft provides. No players are put into silos for extended periods of
time. Contradicting goals serve a creative and narrative-driven goal. One could imagine
though that private back channels exist, where surprises are managed and boundaries
are discussed. Agency itself is subsumed through stewardship.
In a Systems Event context, this could be intentionally replicated by ‘Red Teaming’.[a]
A system would be designed to be tested by another group that assumes an antagonistic
role, then report their assessment. In cybersecurity, ethical hackers have the same skills
and tools as malicious ones, but their goals are non-destructive.
They operate with
permission from the organization while following a code of conduct.
Hermitcraft and similar SMPs are quite systems oriented due to their long running
seasons.
Hermitcraft is composed of over twenty members, whose presence helps to
multiply the efforts of the individual. There is no siloing of players.
Survival Multiplayer Servers that focus on PvP, particularly siloed events like the
civilization events hosted by Ish, rely on balanced teams and legible, predetermined
structured systems from the organizers. The Systems Event lacked the structural support
for both systems and for PvP. Members of the TSE were left to their own subtextual
understanding and failure modelling. For Ordonia, we largely lost sight of the goal as we
were carrying a debt from our exploration phase that we had difficulty fulfilling, and we
were managing more internal and diplomatic tasks.
1.7.2
The question of war
The question of war was something that wasn’t fully clear for us. There wasn’t much to
go off of in official documentation of what war means, the stakes of war, the period, and
should it be a bilateral or unilateral ‘declaration’. Was war just another testing ground,
or was it part of the aim of the event in itself, as opposing factions are prone to do?
Applications were supposedly screened against people who were ‘too PvP focused’,
yet war wasn’t taken off the table. It was another thing left for the ‘vanilla’ or ‘archaic’
feel – undefined and underbaked axioms that were counterproductive to the event. It
was something you could do, if you want.
But the event couldn’t support a war-based factional narrative. There was no hard-
core mode, unbalanced starting conditions, and no guidelines for it. Early on, I suggested
a ‘gentleman’s war’ at the last week of the event. That plan didn’t get very far, as activ-
ity dwindled after the second week. Admittedly, the idea of a unilaterally declared war
was something that seemed out of place in this event to most Ordonians, largely because
of the imbalance in teams and the subtext we have interpreted for the event.
[a]a term used in cybersecurity, where ethical hackers on the behalf of an organization act as antago-
nists, using the tools and exploits of real antagonists

content:
13
We Ordonians were aware of, or at least told, that a sizable portion of Team Alpha
was interested in war ‘for entertainment value’, and that some saw it as a valid zero-sum
path towards victory by the metrics of The Systems Experiment. Individually, we went
back and forth on how much we should interact with Alpha. Some members would be
suspicious and then cool off, only for others to be similarly suspicious. While we felt that
the people of team Alpha were fairly transparent actors, we couldn’t always take what
they said at face value.
1.7.3
The temperature of the tea
Hilo’s role in the event stood out as the host of tea parties early on, where potions were
labelled as ‘Osmanthus Tea’. She became one of the primary builders on the neutral
mushroom island alongside Blaze.
She was seen as a neutral party, yet still at least
nominally a part of Alpha. We were aware that she was collecting information during
the event, and that she had some connection with the Publishing Department.
We recognized that her positions towards both Principals were unique. When there
was little reason for Ordonia to interact with Alpha, her tea parties were a diplomatic
bridge that didn’t need a formal excuse outside itself. It was an invitation to come to
them, see what they have built and developed under diplomatic auspices.
Visitations slowly dropped off as a Visa system implemented by Scorvon came into
effect. This was an early power-grab of his before the election. My first visa was signed
by Phantom_Boi during their power struggle, only for Scorvon to declare it invalid and
request that I fill out another visa. It didn’t take long for most cross-team activity to
switch to the mushroom island, bypassing the need to adhere to antisocial visa policies,
the principle of which were sometimes violated in either direction anyway.
‘Neutral’ positioning aside, we all answered to a team, but we understood Hilo an-
swered to the IMS and the publishing department in a way we weren’t quite sure of
yet. She adopted a stewardly position, but we wouldn’t be sure of what that could have
implied should she or the organizers wanted to take the event in a specific direction. It’s
understood that a need for cross-team proximity was a given, and that we didn’t quite
understand how the organizers planned things, or if they have had much planning at
all. We largely predicted the potential of Team Alpha as Agents rather than stewards or
co-managers.
If we were to view things from the agentic perspective, with war being ‘entertainment’,
we couldn’t realistically provide a satisfactory argument against that.
If war was a
binary checklist item without guidelines or expectations, the results would be predictably
lopsided. So, it wasn’t really about preventing war on its own merits, but making war
potentially expensive. Hilo’s early diplomatic approach made it easier for us to make
connections, trade deals, and social reconnaissance on Team Alpha.
The diplomatic game became one of learning about the members of the other team,
getting candid and one-on-one disclosures, and making trade deals. The problem with
trade deals in this environment though is leverage; each team would desire to have some
kind of leverage over the other, but leverage spent is leverage lost.
The economy of
title: The Ordonian Calculus and the IMS: Stewardship, Agency, and the Economy of Information in The Systems Experiment

content:
14
information proved more valuable than most commodities in this kind of agency-driven
environment, where guidelines and resources were thin.
1.7.4
The fall-off
War wasn’t prevented by diplomatic activity alone, but largely through inactivity. Or-
donia’s systems proved difficult to implement with the scale and resources we ended up
with, our city planning ambitions were poorly planned and mismatched. Some Ordonians
deliberately took a break from the server, while some simply found other things more
interesting, and the ones that stood by burned out.
Alpha, from what we could see, accomplished what they felt they could. The last two
weeks of the event were mostly quiet from their side, with exception of the Nether ex-
pansion and the opening of the End. There was never a moment when enough Ordonians
would be on that declaring a war could be worthwhile.
1.8
Conclusion
We didn’t manage to produce lasting systems that could be shown off, there was nothing
guiding us towards novel cooperative approaches with so few members. There was little
for either team to take back to the IMS, because in this type of loose, vanilla environment,
the most interesting thing is what the other team is doing. Where The Systems Event
may have been productive was as a study of inter- and intra-team dynamics, and as a
lesson of how not to create events.
What could be done for future events depends on the direction that the IMS intends to
take them. Turtle seems to have drawn inspiration from different sources while trying to
design for the broadest appeal, but without more deliberate design, clear communication
and intentions, and a proactive consideration for players’ time, we may see a repeat of
this season’s turn out.
It might be more prudent to risk over-design of future events, so that each season
carries with it an identity, a set of unique problems or challenges, or conditions imposed,
such that the focus becomes player versus environment, or player within the temporary
society. Vanilla doesn’t always mean perfectly vanilla or without guidelines, and anarchy
vanilla has a particularly short set of possible outcomes.
Through the lens of Agency and Stewardship, we may begin to understand how player
behavior relates to the environment they find themselves in. Even when interests don’t
directly align, all parties should be aware of the interests of each other. The Systems
Event was set up with Three Principal Entities all acting within their own interests while
performing a mental calculus of each party’s intentions and efficacy.
It is up to organizers and server administrators to understand and anticipate the re-
sources at their disposal. The system drafts turned into mere homework. The asynchrony
of development and implementation cooled motivation and led to systems misaligned with
the actual conditions of exploitation. Failure to set and clearly communicate guidelines,

goals, and expectations created an environment of uncertainty that was counterproduc-

The design of the event did not clearly define its principles.
We can somewhat
surmise the intentions through the resources and statements that do exist; however, no
true mission statement or theory of design has been made available outside of a points
system. The structure of the event worked against both the resources it had available
and its own design goals.
In conclusion, there should be a theory of Stewardship for the IMS. Any events, exper-

itself is structural, ‘vanilla’, ‘semi-vanilla’, ‘anarchy’, etc., are not neutral choices, nor
are all or most servers in a category going to be the same. These choices are structural
and worthy of scrutiny.
Minecraft Server Theory is still young, but has a solid framework thanks to creators
like Matcha_Tea, Turtlestate, KingGame, Pinecone, and others. We have only started
on what will be a rich tradition for Minecraft as a platform. Player and staff/owner
behavior and motivations are as, if not more, important than the systems themselves.

Article 4
The removal of agency by server
owners and reclaiming player power
Author: matcha_tea. Editor: retrooper. Single-blind peer reviewed.
IMSC: j(2)-ma-8
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23702589
Abstract
Throughout the history of Minecraft servers, there is one system that has remained
the same: leadership. At the top is the server’s owner, the person who has the final
say in any decision made; next are the server’s admins, a group of people whom the
owner trusts to act on their behalf; finally, there are the moderators, who enforce the
server’s rules and maintain conduct in the day-to-day running of the server. I call this
the Traditional structure. This paper argues that this structure is fundamentally flawed
by exploring the core function and purpose of a Minecraft server, which is to create
satisfaction for players on the server. Two key terms are outlined: agency and power,
which are important for understanding why the Traditional structure has and continues
to fail players by examining the issue from the perspective of the Player. This paper
considers the individual player and the lone decision-maker – the owner – as classes in a
hierarchy to better understand the inter-class interactions, removing individual anomalies
in behaviour and allowing readers to understand the problem at a higher level. Finally,
this paper proposes a structure where Players (as a class) have no “need” for the Owner,
as decisions would only be made by Players.
4.1
Introduction
The rigid Owner-Player hierarchy found in Traditional structures has created the most
(monetarily) successful servers in the world (e.g., Hypixel, Mineplex, and Donut SMP).
Both Raid Farms and Minecraft Bloodlines (MCB), the most studied and influential
31
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
32
servers in the field of Minecraft Server Theory (MST), have this rigid top-down structure
of power. It can appear logical, even ideal, to have a few people at the top dictating the
direction of the server and viewing players as numbers and statistics needing improve-
ment.
Such hierarchical systems do not exist in isolation, but in the context of everything
around their creators. Just like the most popular Minecraft servers, the most well-known
real-life corporations also follow this kind of hierarchy – Amazon, Nestle, and Tesla to
name a few.
I will argue in this paper that this hierarchical structure fails to achieve its goal, even
when one thinks solely about higher and higher player counts. To understand why, one
must also reframe one’s thinking of the meaning of “success” for a server, which I argue
should be in terms of player satisfaction instead of other numerical metrics. Following
this, one must also understand that the Traditional structure fails to meet this goal and
is also the reason why the vast majority of servers fail after the Two-Week Phase. I will
discuss an alternative way of thinking about player satisfaction, and by extension, the
success of a server. Moreover, having understood why the Traditional structure fails and
how a different view should be adopted, I will discuss how the same structure deals with
player suggestions and change. I will argue that the unilateral nature of the Owner means
that Players are not satisfied, resulting in the eventual collapse in feelings of excitement
for the server’s potential. Finally, I will lay out a better structure of leadership which
holds Player satisfaction at its core and would yield a more “successful” server.
In this paper, all mentions of “server” can be assumed to mean a Survival Multiplayer
(SMP) server. An SMP is best defined in its components, which includes but is not
limited to:
• Survival gamemode
• Multiplayer
• Focused on player-to-player interaction
• An open and expansive world for players to do as they wish
4.1.1
Use of “satisfaction” in this paper
The word satisfaction is used throughout this paper instead of fun as, ironically, what
gives players satisfaction may not always be fun. Take the example of fighting the Ender
Dragon. It is a difficult fight for the typical player, and one may die several times during
the fight. This is by no means an activity that can objectively and easily be considered
fun, but it brings about satisfaction in that the player continues to engage in the activity
and has fun in the end. One can consider satisfaction to be fun in hindsight, where even
if a player struggled during a difficult part of the game, as long as they came out of it
for the better, they can think in hindsight that they did have fun.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
33
4.2
Existing structures and hierarchies
The current mainstream leadership structure is roughly similar to the following:
(In descending order of power)
Owner > Admin > Moderator > Player
As explained in the next section, this structure is inefficient in achieving player satis-
faction. However, we must first discuss how this structure works in practice and why it
sometimes creates a successful server.
The Owner[a] holds the most power in a server and all decisions must be made with
their approval. As they hold control of the Minecraft server (and usually also the Discord
server that they might have), only they can make changes. Even if it is a decision that
a majority of the leadership team (that is, the Admins and possibly the Moderators,
together with the Owner) supports, only the Owner is able to actually install a mod
or change the game difficulty, for example. This means they have complete autocratic
control over all things, even if they are amicable and adhere to the majority rule. Thus,
I think it is less pertinent to discuss the roles of the Admins and Moderators, as their
power is ultimately given by the Owner.
If a real-life example can aid your understanding, take the United Kingdom – the
King is the de facto head of state. Any law passed by both the Houses of Commons and
Lords must be signed off by the King so that it may become the official law of the land.
Without his rubber stamp, any law coming onto his desk will not be in effect, even if the
entire country supports it.[b]
This is completely and undoubtedly dangerous. The high concentration of power, the
selection of the next leader by the current leader, and the leader’s failure to understand
the experiences of ordinary people compound into a dangerous slope toward detachment
from reality.
Why must an Owner, who is not elected, not chosen, and cannot be held accountable
through any means (as they have the ultimate say and can completely disregard all
dissent), control the entire server? Or really, in concrete terms – how does this ensure
player satisfaction?
In a typical SMP server founded between friends, one of them will be the Owner
who has likely initiated the idea, owning the physical server that the world is hosted on.
Initially, the Owner may decide to ask their Players what kinds of mods and mechanics
they would want present on the server. Thereafter, some players may request a change,
and others may disagree with the requested change. The Owner acts as a mediator in
these cases to make a quick decision based on their own opinion to move the conversation
forwards, as they simply want to have fun with their friends. Here, maintaining a strict
democratic decision-making process is not necessary as the goal is not to boost player
[a]Owner and other terms are capitalised as I am talking about the institution and the class of person,
not specifically the person who embodies the role. This distinction is important as the things I talk
about are inherent to the role and will not change depending on who is in that specific office.
[b]Parliament can, using specific laws, force legislation to be approved.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
34
satisfaction and increase the regular player count; instead, the owner is part of a group
of friends who use their server as a medium to interact and spend time together.
In other words, disagreements in terms of gameplay mechanics can be taken less
seriously due to the server’s goal, so having efficient and unilateral decision-making is
good. Unilateral decision-making may also be more beneficial if all players already know
each other before starting to play – which means discussion and compromise is more
likely to be fruitful.
One may raise the issue that the server’s goal might have been influenced or intro-
duced by the players at the beginning of the server, which means that even if the owner
unilaterally makes executive decisions, it still follows the intention set by the players at
the beginning.
This is true; however, we must remember that goals and ideas shift over time. A
player who suggests, for example, the Copper Rails mod to be installed on the server as
they believe it will increase the uses of copper may later find, after using it for a while,
that it actually decreases the incentive to mine for gold and iron. Here, their opinion on
copper rails may change, but yet, they have no power to change the fact that the mod is
installed.
In order for a server to have broad appeal, ensuring player satisfaction and increasing
its regular player count, two things must be considered: player agency and player power.
I shall define agency as follows:
Agency can be thought of as a player’s inward feeling about whether they
have the power to bring about change effectively on a server—which is a
standard definition.
Power, however, has nuance to its definition in this context, which I shall define as follows:
Typically, power is thought of as something which is direct, physical (or
mental), or radical. However, power can come in many different ways. This
can be power to speak up to a person with more power (e.g., the Owner),
power to influence other players, power to enact practical change, and power
to simply have one’s opinion heard.
Let us first explore a simplified scenario involving a new player who initially enjoys a
server but ultimately decides to leave.
First, the player is intrigued by something on the server. If we take the example
of Raid Farms, this may be its famous wheat currency. They join the server and they
are engaged with this mechanic. As time passes, they notice more things about the new
mechanic that they previously hadn’t, continuing to make them more and more enthused.
Then, the player inevitably finds a mechanic that they are not the most pleased with.
Sticking with our example, the enchanting system has been a large topic of interest and
discussion. At this point, the player feels a lot of agency to be able to do this as they
have a positive view of the server overall, but not yet a lot of power in seeing real change
or feedback.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
35
Next, our newly joined but already dedicated player wants to change their new
favourite server for the better.
They make a suggestion in the server and find that
many agree with them. Here, their feeling of agency continues to rise as their power to
bring about change is affirmed. They also begin to feel more power as they seem to have
invited many people who agree with them, rallying for the change.
The Owner notices this, agrees, and listens to their feedback. We see the peak of
both agency and power here: agency is felt by those who feel strongly about this issue
when the highest authority on the server affirms that their concerns are valid, and power
is felt because they managed to influence this person, who is seen as a role model.
Finally, when the change is implemented, the player might feel unsatisfied, especially
if the implementation does not meet their expectations. The change may not have been
implemented perfectly, or it may even just require one or two more tweaks. However,
at this point, the player’s agency is completely shattered as they feel that they are not
heard, and thus, did not bring about the change they desired.
Not all players decide to leave immediately after this, but it is very likely that some
might. We should also remember that our dedicated new joiner would not leave at this
point, as they feel a sense of loyalty to the server, but the vast majority of players
view a server as a product to be consumed, not an institution or organisation deserving
protection, advancement, and dedication.[a]
In terms of looking at agency and power for player satisfaction, the breaking point
occurred when the Owner, being this perceived bastion of power and being the ultimate
decision-maker, went against the wishes of the players. The players’ individual belief
that the Owner knows what is best for the server, and what steps to take in order to
reach their goal, has been shattered as they themselves put the Owner on this pedestal.
One may argue that the fault is not in having an Owner but in the beliefs of the
Players. However, this ignores the context in which the Players exist – one where the
Owner places themselves in this position of power and status, almost asking to be admired
for their apparent wisdom. Players simply follow this expectation that the Owner must
be looked up to – creating the situation we find ourselves in.
4.3
Pleasing the players
Now that we’ve discussed what typical mainstream servers have as their hierarchy of
power, and the feelings of agency and power individual players have, we shall shift focus
to the Players as a group.
Say that you are the owner of a server – how do you balance your own vision for the
server from before it started with the assumed visions of the players? How can you make
sure the decisions demanded by the players are recognised without allowing them to make
choices that (in your view) harm the server? Is it possible to increase the popularity of
your server without assimilating with the ever-growing number of servers who all have
one, stubborn, goal in their mind – increasing player count?
[a]I recognise that this is an unsupported claim.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
36
In order to answer these questions, you must understand the two weights in play in
any multiplayer server – the view of the players and the view of the server owner.[a] If
the two views are visualised as a two-circle Venn diagram, the area of their intersection
can be thought of as the amount of flexibility an owner has in making decisions – how
much of their own circle they can pick ideas out of. This intersection also represents the
views that both the Owner and the Players have in common.
However, these are weights, meaning that they also possess another property – their
physical mass – or, how important they are perceived to be. This perception can be
held by the server owner regarding players, meaning how much of the players’ opinions
are taken into account when deciding server mechanics, for example. This can also be
a perception held by the players themselves – whether they feel they have a voice in
making decisions.
Four possible situations arise from these two factors which I shall deal with indepen-
dently:
1. Large intersection of views[b] + High weight of player opinion
2. Large intersection of views + Low weight of player opinion
3. Low intersection of views + High weight of player opinion
4. Low intersection of views + Low weight of player opinion
The first case is the optimal case in a hierarchical server – the server owner is satisfied
that their direction for the server lines up with their player base’s opinion, and they are
open to taking the players’ views in consideration when making decisions.
One may argue that the second term is a direct cause of the first term. In other
words, because the owner has a large number of views in common with their players, it is
much easier for the owner to accept them as peers. Although this view seems straightfor-
ward and natural, the two terms are completely independent from each other. Take the
example of a server owner whose direction for their server is popular among the player
base but who does not actively listen to them, instead making decisions independently –
it is simply coincidental that the owner’s actions align with the players’ wants.
The above situation would be representative of the second case – a lot in common,
but the owner acts independently.
It is also important to note that these terms are
fluid – an owner who has a lot in common with their players at the establishment of
the server may not hold the same values or vision for the server after a few months of
operation; similarly, an owner who is receptive to feedback at the start may later find
their player base acting rashly, and thus, decrease the weight on player opinion when
making decisions.
The third case is of a humble and open owner – although their vision is unaligned
with their players’, they are still open to feedback and advice. These owners listen to
[a]In some servers, this may also be the view of the admins, or even moderators. In any case, I refer
to the person, or group of people, who have power to make decisions about the server.
[b]That is, of the server owner and the players.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
37
their players attentively and are usually the ones who are thought of most highly by the
players and considered “one of the people”, creating an equal environment where all views
are respected.
One may argue here that the third case is the optimum. Firstly, despite the differences
in opinion, the owner continues to take the players’ perspectives into account; thus, this
must be the case where the most respect is given – even more than the first case, as the
respect in that case may be fragile. Further, the owner being amicable with their player
base, and the players being amicable with the owner, must mean that a more positive
community is built.
To explain why both arguments fail – or why both positions remain rather inefficient
for the goal of player satisfaction – we must consider them in relation to the goal of a
server.
What is the purpose of a Minecraft server? Or even, what is a Minecraft server?
I will define a server (that is, not only an SMP, e.g., anarchy, geopol) for the purposes
of the following sections as follows:
A multiplayer environment where people involved in the environment, be it
as a moderator or player, work towards a goal that they individually have.
This may be a shared goal, a formally recognised and rigid goal, or even an
informal goal such as “fun”. An “environment” could refer to a Survival world
with the Nether and End locked, or a Creative server with building plots.
Ultimately, servers have a loose goal – and for an SMP, which this paper deals with – this
is fun. The exact definition of fun is not important here, but the fact that this subjective
goal remains desired is of importance.[a]
There are a few things that must be understood to realise the flawed nature of one
figure ruling over an entire server.
Firstly, recognise that players play on a server. Even if the owner plays on the server,
they can also be thought of as a player. The subjective goal of fun needs to be agreed
upon by the majority of the players in order to maximise the amount of fun that any
particular individual may have. This is usually done through discussion between players
either within the server environment itself (in-game) or through external forums, such as
Discord.
Secondly, understand that the players themselves will know best about what they
want. Even when given a private, honest space to share their opinions, some players
will still feel anxious about dissenting against the Owner, whom they perceive as “all-
knowing”.
Further, no amount of oversight or observation by the owner may be able to represent
all player opinions. Even if the owner plays on the server regularly and engages with
the community as a normal player, they will still have a skewed or biased view of the
server. There is also the question of differential treatment by players towards the owner
[a]Note that fun and satisfaction are not the same idea. Fun is a broad and generally undefined word
used to describe a “vibe” players get when they are feeling satisfied on a server. Because it is unspecific
and relating to an emotion, I separate these.
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
38
when they are playing, which will also exaggerate the positive aspects of the players and
diminish the negative ones.
One can argue that if the owner plays on an “alt account”, they will be able to get a
true experience on the server; however, this will also produce a biased result depending
on the owner’s own play style, influencing whom they interact with.
Thirdly, many players often put forward suggestions for changing a server by dis-
cussing them among themselves, then bringing those suggestions forward to the owner
– usually through more influential or well-known players who may have sway over the
owner. However, this is an inefficient way of creating change.
Fourthly, even if the owner always does approve of all suggestions, there may be
disagreement in the implementation of the suggestions. An owner will always have a
skewed view of their server, as mentioned above, due to their status and role in the
power hierarchy.
This may have the effect of creating more harm than good, as the
players could feel that their desires are not being fulfilled – but at the same time, the
owner can develop a perception that their work is not being valued and that implementing
player suggestions is a waste of time.[a] Consequently, this creates a negative feedback
loop that causes the area of intersection between the Owner and the Players to shrink,
leading to the opinion of the Players being given less weight, until the point where the
two classes are completely polarised and players begin to leave.
Having considered these points, one can still find a commonality between them –
which is that all decisions could be made by the owner. One may suggest that this results
in quick, efficient decision-making and less bureaucracy, allowing players to experience
server changes more quickly and accelerating the feedback loop.[b] This may also mean
that players have a higher likelihood (due to how frequently opportunities to show agency
arise) of feeling satisfaction. All processes have trade-offs, and this example is one that
we must deal with.
In order to please players and restore their power, inefficiency is a necessary evil. As
we’ve established, only players know best what they want in a server, and any other
person or group of people making decisions for them in the name of “knowing better” is
more inefficient as it will not deliver a satisfactory result and will require more iterations
of the feedback loop – this is compared to the often tedious and long-drawn nature
of discussion and collective decision making, but it almost always guarantees a more
satisfactory result.
The fact that players collectively make these decisions also means that discussions
can be more civil as every person has equal amounts of power, sharing a unifying goal
that is constructive – compared to the unifying, but unhelpfully critical, goal that players
may have against the owner.
One could construct a strong argument that setting up a new server and establishing
new leadership can provide an entirely clean slate for a more stable form of leadership.
[a]Of course, not every owner will think the same. However, for the purposes of this paper, I shall use
a generalisation of the worst-case-scenario where applicable.
[b]The feedback loop is the following: problem →solution identified →change →player feedback →
(repeat)
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
39
One fault in this argument is that the players’ emotional attachment to the world remains
overlooked. This means a brand-new world must be created. Players must re-establish
relationships, create new cultural landmarks, and invent new in-jokes about the server.
This process is physically exhausting, mentally exhausting, and most importantly: it
decreases satisfaction monumentally.
Further, I believe the revolution (so to say) of the Players against the Owner can
deliver even more satisfaction than resetting everything. Server cultures stay in place,
relationships remain stable (if not reinforced), and the world stays the same. If, even-
tually, the Players do overthrow the Owner, a new vibrant culture of daily discussion –
which players know will at least not be a waste of time – can drive players’ motivation to
play and participate on the server. This is in contrast to there being an issue on a server
with a Traditional structure, where a player may try to create change before ultimately
giving up.
4.4
Reclaiming player power
The players’ power can, and must be, reclaimed. The system of operating a server where
this is achieved is the Co-operative system.
Due to the already established monopoly of the Owner over the Players, it is essential
that the Players unite against the Owner. There must be no doubt between players that
what they are against is an (almost) immovable force who has control over their server
and their community. The Players must realise that as long as they have an owner, their
feelings of agency will be capped at a certain level due to the presence of an immovable
obstacle to gaining ultimate collective power.
This is where celebrity players come in – these people have the most agency (as they
already know that they are popular amongst other players), and the most power (as they
are also recognised personally by the owner), which allows them to influence both the
classes effectively. The influence they perform leads to increased feelings of agency, which
in turn also boosts their own satisfaction – which can lead to a positive feedback loop,
allowing them to influence the owner even more.
I envision this to be a long, tedious, and very difficult process: when you try to dispel
the myth of “efficiency” and “wisdom” of the Owner to a recipient who has only ever known
the status-quo, you will meet great resistance. However, once much of the Players have
been educated about these matters, they should constantly and without hesitation repeat
the same, commonly agreed-upon message of disapproval to show their unity against the
Owner. The Players shall force the Owner to be removed and immediately set up concrete
infrastructure within the Discord server (or other means of communication) to establish
the following as a minimum:[a]
1. An open, free, and respectful space for debate and discussion
2. Direct voting on server mechanics, which can be initiated by any player
[a]Please keep in mind that this should not be taken as a fully planned out manifesto – this paper
simply lays the foundation for its necessity.

40
3. An Executive Council chosen by lottery to implement approved changes
The first is essential for any Player-owned server, as the basis of the entire concept is
for players to be able to discuss amongst themselves and enact change directly to other
members of the same class; a safe space for all players to participate in this process is
absolutely necessary. This space must be inclusive of all and do its best to give equal
weight and time to all voices, no matter how famous, influential, or veteran. However,
at the same time, members of the Executive Council must not be able to participate in
debate, and they must be politically neutral because of their role, which requires them to
be disinterested and unbiased parties whose job is simply to carry out the agreed-upon
wishes of the Players.
This will also cement the fact that agency and satisfaction are the primary goals
of a co-operative server. If players feel that they are able to drive change (and if they
truly can drive change), they will feel like they have agency. Similarly, if there is a lower
barrier to enjoying oneself on the server, satisfaction will come about more easily.
The second of the three-legged stool allows for the results of these debates to be carried
out. Direct voting means that every player’s vote is equal and meaningful. Decisions
by referendum also avoid the problem that ultimately rises from using a representative
system, which gives certain players an elevated position, mimicking the Owner. The
latter part of this point enshrines the equal right and power of every player to be able to
create change. In terms of agency and power, this reaffirms both.
This right also creates opportunities for abuse and trolling, as a newly joined troll has
the exact same power as a two-year veteran. However, this right is essential to maintain a
“no exceptions” culture when it comes to having the right to say something is wrong, and
to change it, starting from oneself. To address this risk, a simple majority vote could be
conducted, serving as a preliminary check before continuing to debate a proposed issue
or solution.
The final point ensures that the debates held were not pointless and that a team of
regular players – not a dictatorial entity like the Owner – will carry out the practical
steps needed implement a new change.
This Executive Council is chosen by lottery,
meaning that it is not disproportionately filled with self-sorting players who may have
a certain bias or obsession with the server’s operations, making them interested parties
and likely ineffective at being unbiased when carrying out the necessary, practical work.
This also serves as a safeguard against corruption, as the players who bring a proposal
to the Council cannot influence it without knowing who is on the Council.
A random chance of being on the Council also means that a culture of equality is
established.
Because serving on it is normalised, players begin to feel like part of a
political culture where everyone is truly seen and treated as equal.
4.5
Caveat for this system
It is important to note that, just like many server proposals, one that focuses on restoring
agency and power may not always be the best for the players. Take the example of a
title: The removal of agency by server owners and reclaiming player power

content:
41
Vanilla UHC server – there are a set of rules, some mods, and everything else is set in
stone. Not only are the Players’ opinions not heard or cared about, but they are not
given any weight either. The established culture within the server is that “it is what it is”,
and making changes is irrelevant. The prevailing view is that a server built on survival,
competition, PvP, and defending your base does not require players to get involved with
how it is managed.
Although total disregard for player feedback remains rare, servers with concrete and
specific goals face a significant challenge.
It is difficult to justify introducing player-
led decision-making on these servers, even regarding peripheral issues where the players
might actually make better decisions.
4.6
Conclusion
In this paper, we’ve discussed existing hierarchical structures of leadership, player satis-
faction regarding agency and power, and the intersections of Player and Owner views. We
also assessed how much weight these views hold for the Owner and provided a template
for how Players can take back ownership of their servers.
4.7
Acknowledgements
Thanks to Harlow for giving me feedback on the first draft of this paper. I would also like
to thank the two anonymous reviewers and retrooper, the editor, who all gave extensive
feedback on the manuscript.

No conflict of interest and no AI use have been declared.

Article 2

Minecraft: The Systems Experiment
Findings
Author: Mila. Editors: Harlow and retrooper. Peer reviewed.
IMSC: j(2)-mia-1
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23702314
Abstract
The Minecraft world is an example of a digital space that closely resembles our real world.
TSE specifically, just like many other multiplayer servers, is an ideal place to observe
said similarities. By finding connections between both worlds involving phenomena such
as how power is distributed, diplomacy handled, or how the world progresses, we can
also use this information to make predictions about events involving those topics. This
can be achieved through a simple process involving a little bit of history and logic.
2.1
The commons of different worlds
In a world where the internet bridges large distances and connects individuals through-
out the globe, there are bound to be certain applications that will simulate the world
itself. Games like Minecraft that allow players to gather and build cultures and gov-
ernments represent this perfectly; however, many people fail to realize how similar a
simple game can match our large and complex society. In the instance of the Systems
Experiment server, a multiplayer Minecraft server with two opposing “countries”, three
particular topics stood out to strongly resemble their real-world counterparts. By gath-
ering the perspectives of the majority of individuals per team and contrasting them with
movements and popular opinions in the real-world, the resemblance between a Minecraft
18
title: Society and Governance Parallels in Minecraft: The Systems Experiment Findings

content:
19
society and our real-world societies is evident. By the end of the experiment, many play-
ers witnessed the same entropy that came with technology, as well as many diplomatic
events that could only be synthesized by one’s experiences in the real-world. With these
parallels drawn, people can attempt to explain real-world phenomena, explore the causes
of important events, and even make their own predictions about the world we live in.
Although power is a highly debated topic, for the sake of this article, we can describe
power as how capable a person is of changing the behaviors of a group of people. In our
world, power is distributed and held in many different ways, with examples ranging from
influencers on social media, to people with enough power to conceal themselves from
public knowledge. One concentration of power, however, is visible in both TSE and real
life—that being politicians. In real life, politicians obtain power through public support,
control of resources, and by utilizing their ability to change government policy. To de-
termine whether the leadership roles in the IMS experiment match those of politicians,
we must draw connections between these aspects.
To start, within the experiment server, both teams required their leaders to hold a
sufficient amount of support from their people. This can be particularly seen with Team
Alpha’s first election on July 11, 2026, where Phantom won over Scorvon in a poll. This
was achieved partially in his speech, where his promises for stability and his anti-war
emphasis reflected the concerns of the people, similar to real life campaigns. Actions
also are involved, as some voters might have cast doubt on Scorvon’s own pro-diplomatic
claims after overhearing his threats toward Ordonia. Next, itistiff and Llama Amongus,
in charge of Team Ordonia’s relations with Team Alpha, were able to permit the al-
location of resources to provide trade to team Alpha. We will soon see why they did
this, but said trade still holds a considerable amount of diplomatic power, as its use (or
lack of it) can determine friends, foes, or everything in between. In instances of chang-
ing government policy, leaders like Scorvon, Phantom, and Pheelix signed agreements
espionage, trade, and etiquette. At its core, agreements like these limit or expand the
freedoms of players/people for a key change – mutual benefit. This benefit can boost
both teams in many ways, while strengthening the relationship between the leaders and
the populations, which is also useful for diplomacy. With these connections made, we
can safely conclude that there is at least one major similarity in powerholders between
the real world and TSE, however, we can also speculate about several other sources of
power between the two worlds.
An apparent pattern that occurs in almost any world is material wealth. Especially
in games like Minecraft where “grinding” can be used to obtain resources, people often
resort to obtaining a surplus of materials or currency to gain power. With the use of ma-
terial, this power can come in different forms, whether that be militaristic power (hiring
soldiers/buying gear) or political power (lobbying/handouts). Overall, since power (or its
use of it) can be a major factor in deciding actions or consequences in both worlds, this
will aid the connection between the two worlds as well as predictions regarding politics.
Although wars in Minecraft are by no means the same as those in real life, the
similar effects of war (death, destruction, loss of materials) makes diplomacy strikingly
similar in both worlds. For a base definition of diplomacy, we could say that countries use
title: Society and Governance Parallels in Minecraft: The Systems Experiment Findings

content:
20
communication, compromise, and peacebuilding to prevent conflicts and resolve incidents.
Although partially kept secret in TSE, these same three tactics could be seen being used
by the leaders of team Alpha, the leader of team Ordonia, and the diplomatic board of
team Ordonia. To start, by interviewing a couple of members of Ordonia (who I will keep
anonymous in this article), they have admitted to using trade deals to try and prevent
Alpha from wanting a war. This is a good example of peacebuilding, and a popular
real-world tactic known as appeasement. Similarly to countries utilizing appeasement,
Ordonia simply did not have the manpower or the resources to compete with Alpha
militaristically, leading them to resort to trade to prevent the war entirely. There were
also instances of meetings where both teams communicated about trades, issues, and the
war they were trying to prevent. These were rather popular, to the extent that Team
Alpha built a meeting place in their town hall to host them. Notably, it was both large
and decorated, either to impress Ordonian diplomats and any spectators, or to ensure
safety and convenience when hosting a meeting. This also took place to a lesser extent
in smaller visits like tea parties, which were not exactly diplomatic oriented, but still
served as proper communication and as an opportunity to build relations between teams
at a personal level, which cannot be easily achieved with deals or diplomatic visits.
There have also been instances of compromise taking place within these meetings,
specifically about policies and agreements that the two teams have created and upheld
throughout the server. A good example of this would be how team Ordonia compromised
to let team Alpha enter their territory, on the condition that any Alpha players visiting
would announce themselves and keep their locator bar on. In terms of this agreement, it
was much less implemented as a way to avoid war than a simple courtesy for Team Alpha
as a whole. Courtesies such as this compromise can greatly affect opinions and relations,
so they occasionally will be performed to improve one’s image instead of genuine goodwill.
As the event starts to come to a close (as of writing this article), it appears that these
methods of diplomacy have worked, as a war has not started, and there is not any motive
or motivation to start one in the remaining time. This connection can also serve a good
purpose, as being able to predict wars and fights will aid the understanding of the players
and the server better.
As mentioned in the introduction of this article, there has been an observable entropy
linked with in-game progression, which is similar to the side effects we see with technology
advancement in the real-world. To understand this fully, we must first look at how our
world was affected by technology.
At the surface level, it has improved our lives –
people can live comfortably in soft mattresses and fancy smart homes, with technological
efficiency in almost every corner of the world. The hard, dirty jobs have been replaced by
large machinery that can automate grueling tasks at the press of a button, and discoveries
like flight and electricity have made accomplishments that our ancestors could not even
dream of. This is comparable to advancements in Minecraft too, with the unlocking of
new resources like netherite, improvements in farms such as trading halls, and new items
such as elytras. The most obvious drawback to new technology and improvements is the
improvement of war.

content:
21
Wars can be fought with brutal efficiency, with machine guns consecutively killing
hundreds of people, and bombs being dropped to raze cities in mere seconds. Again,
the same exists in Minecraft. Maces and wind charges can deal damage that no other
weapon can, and massive redstone machines can be sent through the map, blowing up
everything in their way. To most, this would seem as an appropriate consequence for the
progression of technology, however, there are still much darker consequences that little
realize until it is too late.
2.2
Finding use in patterns
With the evolution of society, depression, and other mental health issues have been
rapidly increasing. (Hidaka, 2012) People’s lives have been watered down to 9-5 jobs,
with the rest of people’s time spent idly watching TV, playing games, or being on social
media. (Malinsky, 2026) This too is present in Minecraft, particularly when people get
bored and burn out in the later stages of a server, rather than in the start of a fresh
server. After all, this mainly happens after there is nothing new to do, or when people
lose motivation to continue playing. A part of this is that the same technology – that
sought to improve lives and automate the game – strips the joy and risk out of simple
adventures and daily activities. In this regard, machines like auto miners or raid farms
automatically harvest resources rather than having the player earn them, making it a
repetitive clicking session instead of a thrilling outing. People can also burn out from the
work, as the bigger end-game projects can be the same repetitive grinding we see in real
life jobs. Several players fell victim to this in TSE. For example, one player (who will
remain anonymous) experienced burnout from trying to figure out late-game redstone.
But at the end of the day, sometimes there are still simple pleasures. After all, there is
nothing quite like having a simple cup of tea in Minecraft, or in real-life.
Now that several key connections have been established, they can be used to predict
certain related aspects about both Minecraft and real-life. To perform this, simply start
by viewing a scenario in a “cause and effect” sort of way. Although being a simplified
process, if supplemented with the correct data, it can utilize the past to provide a result.
The past, being a useful tool, can be used to see many human behavioral patterns.
Human history particularly is also one of the largest and most accessible pasts, making
it accessible and plentiful. For a hypothetical scenario, let’s start with:
Cause: Tensions are very high between team Alpha and team Ordonia Effect:
???
To fill in the effect, all we would need to do is ask ourselves “if two countries had
high tensions, what would they do in real life?” Then, using our historical knowledge, or
knowledge about the world in the present world, we can fill in:
Cause: Tensions are very high between team Alpha and team Ordonia Effect:
Both teams will attempt to use diplomacy to ease the tensions.

Obviously, we cannot be certain if this is accurate at face value. If the cause is more
specific (e.g., motives, amounts of resources already, etc.), the effect will also be more
specific, and with predictions, even if you had a surplus of data for your cause, you can
never be 100% sure about your effect.
2.3
Conclusion
All in all, the connections we can draw between the world of TSE and the physical
world and the subsequent predictions only mark the start of what we can achieve with
pattern recognition and an observant eye.
Looking closely, it’s also not hard to see
common themes like power, diplomacy, and technology in other player-driven games too.
However, just remember that even the comforting, blocky landscape of Minecraft can
still be strikingly similar to the outside world we all know.
