Article 3
Political Philosophy Is Useless for
the Study of Servers
Author: Moldypizzar0ll. Editor: retrooper. Single-blind peer reviewed.
IMSC: j(2)-ml-2
DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23702491
Abstract
Players of sandbox games in virtual worlds are often inclined to think that the same social
phenomena that spring up in real life are applicable to player-to-player interactions in
game; further, that these interactions are often governed by broader moral or ethical
principles that reflect those of the real world. Thus, for many it makes sense to apply
political philosophy to these games, since they appear to give us a window into how
these systems spring up in the real world. Minecraft is perhaps the clearest example;
because of its open-ended structure, players consider it to be an ideal environment for
simulating and theorizing about political communities. However, I will argue that insofar
as Minecraft presupposes ideal conditions which players must then constrain themselves,
political philosophy can only engage in a descriptive, not normative, role in the study of
communities on Minecraft servers.
3.1
Introduction
Minecraft servers are interesting in myriad ways, not least due to the fact that we tend
to think that they provide insights into how people behave under peculiar circumstances.
Insofar as we think this to be the case, we are also tempted to make prescriptions for
how those people ought to behave. To engage in a community is not just to engage in a
descriptive project, in which the practices of the community are described and represented
in detail, but also to engage in a normative one in which a certain level of institutional
development and social coherence is needed to ensure that things are in order within
23
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
24
the community. Surely there would be few who would say that these assumptions are
unreasonable; and from them we may be tempted to derive the notion that our ways of
understanding what prescriptions we are beholden to in the real world, especially those
that pertain to the political sphere, may also apply to communities broadly; Minecraft
servers being no exception. Hence, our tendency to apply political philosophy to virtual
worlds.
I will argue here, however, that many of these intuitions are mistaken; that, in fact,
most of the questions with which political philosophy deals are scarcely of importance
for understanding what goes on in Minecraft servers (though the case may be made for
other games, I will limit the scope of this argument to Minecraft). In essence, politi-
cal philosophy aims to generate normative prescriptions that apply to political societies,
i.e., prescriptions that apply both to authorities (if one believes the set of legitimate
authorities to be nonempty), and to people following those authorities. These prescrip-
tions are motivated by real-world constraints, while communities in Minecraft are not
so constrained; the place of political philosophy in Minecraft is thus posterior, rather
than anterior, to what people ought to do; for political philosophy usually only serves
to present what is possible to the players in terms of the kind of situation they would
like to find themselves in rather than as a legitimate, normatively-binding force that acts
upon them. Whatever normatively binding forces actually exist, exist on the level of
individuals rather than on the level of a political community.
3.2
The purview of political philosophy
3.2.1
Resource distribution
In the first place, much of political philosophy is centered around how to distribute
resources fairly. There are competing views, even prior to strictly political ones, as to
how adequate distributions are to be achieved. Pure egalitarians argue that resources
should be distributed equally across the population without exception. Luck egalitarians
argue much the same and hold that differences in outcomes across individuals should be
a function only of any given individual’s own choices. Prioritarians argue that benefits
given to the least well-off should be weighed more than those given to those better-
off. (Parfit, 1997) There are, of course, different ethical theories that provide justification
for various political theories. The prioritarian, for example, may be motivated by the
utilitarian consideration that one should aim to maximize the amount of good done for
the greatest number of individuals, which means giving benefits to the least well-off.
Others may not be moved by utilitarianism and instead view the consequences of an
action simply as a reason, yet not a final reason for doing something. In Anscombe’s
example, (Anscombe, 1967) five people are stranded on one island and one person on
another; you manage to spot both islands and decide to save the one person.
The
five people, according to Anscombe, do not have a claim to having been wronged; for
someone was indeed saved, and the rescuer did not decide not to save anyone.
She
discusses another example, more explicitly related to the distribution of resources. One
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
25
person suffers from a fatal illness, and a group of five suffer from the same illness. A
single vial of an antidote is available; except the former person requires the entire vial
to be cured, and the latter five each require one-fifth of the vial to be cured. No-one is
wronged, Anscombe concludes, if one decides to give the one person the entire vial rather
than saving the five. Is this a fair use of resources? Now, political considerations are, at
bottom, ethical considerations. But there is disagreement with respect to how one moves
from the ethical to the political. A plausible answer is that the ethical becomes the
political when resources are involved on a sufficient scale—viz., when certain patterns of
distribution may be considered more just than others. Whatever normative prescriptions
follow, then, aim to achieve such distributions.
What we should note at this point is not strictly anything having to do with the
individual views given here. Rather, we should note that the central aim of ethics is
to remedy an existing state of affairs, call this A, via some theory so as to achieve a
fairer, more just state of affairs; call this B. Different views have different verdicts on
how to get from A to B, and what B would actually look like. Some, such as Anscombe,
do not believe B to be wholly determined by the consequences of actions, and thus
does not necessarily prescribe that B, for a good ethical theory, always supervenes on
consequences. Others, such as Parfit, would disagree. (Parfit, 1984) One of the plausible,
though perhaps not exhaustive, ways in which a view can conceive this move from mere
ethical prescriptions to talk of the political (taken in the philosophical sense) is in terms
of the distribution of resources.
In Minecraft servers, however, things work differently. Assuming we examine a vanilla
server in its infancy, its initial conditions are starkly different than any “initial” state of
affairs in the real-world. Players are hidden behind a Rawlsian “veil of ignorance”, in
which their physical real-world characteristics are largely stripped away and only their
in-game capabilities and knowledge remain.[a] (Rawls, 1971, p. 10) The distribution of
resources, moreover, is nominally equal. The Rawlsian metaphor here breaks down, as we
cannot benefit the least well-off having assumed the veil of ignorance if the distribution
of resources past a certain point is scarcely of importance. Of course, there may exist a
scarcity of labor;[b] but there is little one cannot acquire with reasonable effort. Others
have noticed this feature of the game, and many agree that the player is almost completely
autonomous resource-wise. What are the possibilities, then, if one wants to make a server
interesting? The traditional problems that drop out from the assumptions of real-world
political philosophy do not really drop out in the case of Minecraft. Theoretically, each
player can act autonomously resource-wise, and questions concerning how to distribute
resources fairly do not arise. We are missing, however, the fact that this is precisely
why political philosophy does not have any normative pull in Minecraft, at least in the
case of resource distribution. For the good server owner knows that an effective way
to motivate interest in a server is to create problems.
The server owner may place
[a]Of course, their mental capacities, memories, previous relationships, etc., still remain. What matters
is that each player has the capacity to affect and derive resources from the world similarly, which is not
so in the real world.
[b]I’m indebted to Snorka for this observation.
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
26
borders on the world so as to limit the number of resources available; cap the number
of valuable items in circulation; limit movement within a region to force cooperation;
etc. It is only here that the traditional problems pop out. Indeed, if, for example, the
world border is limited, one has to figure out the ideal distribution. But because such
artificial constraints can only be generated by presupposing what the ideal distribution
actually is (i.e., something like a server’s unaltered state where players are completely
resource-autonomous), the solution is already baked into the design. While real-world
political philosophy is indeterminate as to what the ideal state of affairs (B) would look
like from the perspective of a determinate state of affairs (A), a Minecraft server has to
create indeterminacy by presupposing what the ideal conditions are and subsequently
imposing constraints. Political philosophy, then, is only useful for people invested in the
server insofar as the ones in charge of the server use it to design the server, rather than
provide normative prescriptions for those within it. At that point, however, it ceases
being political philosophy.
Political philosophy gets its normativity precisely because the state of affairs towards
which it aims is indeterminate and hazy. We ought to do X in part because the possibility
of X coming about is a possibility, not an actuality. We cannot say that one ought to
do something given that the state of affairs with which they are charged with realizing
has already come about.[a] In server design, by contrast, the tools political philosophy
has at its disposal can only be cashed out in terms of descriptions. When the server
owner imposes a world border, given what we know about what is valuable in the game,
what the players ought to do is a foregone conclusion. We can only observe them going
through the motions of playing within the world, knowing what the optimal decision
procedures are for them already given the constraints. Now, the claim is not that the
players are completely predictable; of course, players often do things they ought not to do
(e.g., killing other players, griefing, hoarding, etc.), but that is not what is at stake here.
The claim is that normative prescriptions cease being interesting as the raison d’etre
of a community when the structures that organize that community already presuppose
what people ought to do in the first place. Political philosophy in this case becomes an
explanation for a state of affairs, rather than a guide for action so as to reach a different
state of affairs.
3.2.2
The state
Take another salient topic in political philosophy: namely, the ideal position and configu-
ration of the state. This is an issue with a distinguished history; its first true treatments
may be found in Plato and Aristotle. The former thought the ideal form of political
organization to consist of philosopher-rulers who, having been trained to seek truth and
inquire into the nature of things (via the Forms), would be the best suited to manage a
polity. (Plato, 1968) The latter (who was not terribly keen on the Forms) was concerned
[a]N.B. This is distinct from normative prescriptions which say that one ought to repeat certain actions
so as to bring a certain state of affairs about continuously (e.g., continuously donating one tenth of your
wealth to charity). The claim here pertains only to past states of affairs, which cannot be altered.
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
27
with the structure and size of the state as much as he was with what it ought to do.
Should we have a monarch, in which only one individual rules, an aristocracy in which
only a few rule, or a constitution[a] in which the majority rule? Aristotle (2008) thought
a benevolent king to be the most ideal, though a constitution to be the most practical
and just. Others were concerned with the function and limits of the state. Should the
state wield unlimited power, or should it have checks and balances? Should we accept
the latter, what kinds of checks should we impose? Hobbes was willing to accept the
former; (Hobbes, 1994) others like Montesquieu and Nozick the latter. Sovereignty may
be something that, by virtue of its nature, is indivisible—where any division in the power
of the sovereign may lead us to suppose that whatever entities exist after the division
are not sovereign at all. Given that an undivided, all-powerful sovereign is a preferable
sort of political organization to an anarchic state of nature, we should opt for the for-
mer. This is the essence of Hobbes’s argument. Nozick is a good foil; for he argues that
the sole permissible functions of the state are to enforce contracts and protect its sub-
jects. (Nozick, 1974) Beyond this point, the state is morally unjustified in doing anything
further. Others believe that the state should not exist at all, or at least that there are
no legitimate authorities.
Again, the important thing to note here is that the normative prescriptions we put
to states, whether it be with respect to its size, limits, or constitution, are a product of
constraint. Political philosophers argue that we ought to move from one state of affairs
to another, given the inadequacy of the preceding state of affairs. Minecraft, by contrast,
can always be adequate. We cannot prescribe how a state should look like in the game
so much as one willingly and consciously participates in its construction. There is no
normative pull. If we want a particular sort of state to arise in the game, we must make
the conditions suitable for its realization. We would not be concerned with what we
ought to do in order to realize high-level goods, e.g., maximizing the satisfaction of the
players, setting up the right kind of state, or distributing resources in the most efficient
manner; for the best way to do that, presumably, is to let everyone run amok and do
whatever they wish. Because of the game’s design as a sandbox, such ends are already
built into the game. Minecraft is already a maximizing tool, since, ceteris paribus, it lets
the player do whatever they want. Whatever political constraints there are appear to
be artificial and scarcely normative. The place of political philosophy, then, if there is
any, is in the realm of institutional design; of designing certain situations so as to achieve
certain objectives and outcomes. Its place is not in offering us any novelties about what
we ought to do in certain situations, since the game, at least politically, already gives us
solutions.
[a]Aristotle used the term “democracy” to refer to the degenerate form of a constitution, in which the
tyranny of the majority prevails. One may think of a “constitution” as something like a just, modern-day
democracy. Additionally, for the three “just” versions of the possible configurations of the state, Aristotle
posits an “unjust” mirror image of each of those forms; namely: tyranny for monarchy, oligarchy for
aristocracy, and democracy for the constitution.
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
28
3.3
Ethics, generally considered
Now, in addition to this claim I also sought to claim something else; namely, that what-
ever normative prescriptions we can cash out of Minecraft servers, occur on the level
of individuals rather than political communities. More specifically, normative ethics as
applied to individuals still holds up in the presence of changes in institutional design. We
have observed that a political community in Minecraft must in large part be designed
so as to achieve certain specifications and objectives; for such communities would not
otherwise have arisen. Normative relations between individuals, however, are scarcely
so designed. Although changes in an external situation can enforce certain changes on
the entirety of a community, the relations between individuals do not necessarily change
character as a result; normative prescriptions between them still have the same charac-
ter. For example, if it is generally permitted on a server for players to kill each other,
this does not necessarily make it morally permissible for individuals to kill each other in
turn. I may still have an obligation to my friend to refrain from killing them as far as
killing them would cause them harm in-game (and in certain exceptional circumstances,
in the real world). But the institutional design of the server has no bearing whatsoever
on whether my killing my friend is permissible or impermissible. What institutional de-
sign can do is make certain actions more or less acceptable; for what matters in the case
of institutional design is upholding the design itself, not necessarily maximizing a good.
Hence breaking or following certain precepts may gain or lose one repute or respect. But
this has no real normative import. If one desired to implement a monarchical system on
a server, the question of whether the monarchy is, in fact, implemented can be pulled
apart entirely from whether this arrangement benefits the players substantially. This is
completely unlike the real world, wherein the maintenance of a state of affairs indeed has
a direct bearing on the well-being of its participants.
To clarify: suppose that considerations of institutional design led us to desire the
realization of a pattern, P, within a server. We may also suppose that the purpose of a
server is to complete some objective, O, where O takes into account in some measure the
well-being of the participants, or some other ethically relevant aspect of the participants’
experience in the server. The claim is that O is not necessarily dependent on the mere
realization, or process of realizing P. For the relation is actually inverted; depending
on the objective of the server, the institutional design will reflect that objective.
P,
in fact, depends on O; and this dependence prefigures the relevant politico-philosophical
precepts that account for what people ought to do once this pattern is established. Hence,
any deviation from P can be accounted for by the fact that it may just reflect O more
satisfactorily. Ethics in general, as it applies to the individual player, can figure in since
that is precisely what determines the shape of O. It is important not to conflate such
prescriptions with politico-philosophical ones.
It still makes perfect logical sense, for
instance, to talk about the aggregate utility of a group of agents without invoking the
state or authority in general, and consequentialist and nonconsequentialist ethics without
patterns of resource distribution.
title: Political Philosophy Is Useless for the Study of Servers

content:
29
These conclusions are intuitively absurd. However, I am not claiming that political
philosophy is useless in Minecraft in general. Rather, I am claiming that it is not useful
when we consider the study of human behavior in Minecraft servers specifically.
Of
course, were Minecraft like the real world to a high degree of accuracy, it would certainly
be useful. But presumably the study of these pockets of human interaction is not the
study of what individuals ought to do, but rather of what they do. What they ought to
do can only be cashed out at the level of the individual, as far as they are charged with
the presence of other players with whom they interact. But when it comes to the general
design of the server in which they find themselves, any large-scale normative prescriptions
that could hope to approximate anything that real-world political philosophy would offer
vanish—and for the simple reason that one can theoretically realize whatever state of
affairs they want within the game.
3.4
Concluding thoughts
What we find interesting about applying political philosophy to Minecraft is not, as our
intuitions may tell us enticingly, the fact that we find moral prescriptions for what people
should do under certain circumstances.
Rather, what we find interesting is isolating
certain facets of human behavior that we know to be present already and seeing them play
out in real time without real-world consequences. Political philosophy cannot provide
anything for the game for precisely this reason. When designing servers, or places where
people coexist in general, one must inevitably come up against a form of the old Hegelian
problem that a movement of a state of affairs is not necessary but imposes its necessity.
In Minecraft servers, the ethical never becomes the political; for the political is imposed,
not made.
3.5
Declarations

Running a coup d'etat: a look at the means 
By: Freeve4
IMSC: S-F4-1
For several years, I’ve been observing a specific player archetype I call the “Initiator”; An 
ambitious player who starts many events within a server and can lead to extreme changes if 
harnessed correctly. Throughout several different servers, I’ve seen players with varying degrees 
of ambition; some merely made dents of chaos, but others have blown craters within a server’s 
trajectory. While I am still working on the theory of this type of player, I have decided to tell the 
recent tale of how an initiator became a key figure in the complete takeover of a Minecraft 
server’s admin team and ownership. 
The story starts roughly a year after the server’s initial creation. After continuous effort, I 
became the sole provider of the server hardware, which gave me the leverage needed to enter the 
second highest spot in the admin team. Since the first season of the server, I had been 
experiencing the effects of poor moderation and management. Having had several building 
projects ruined over several seasons — one of which was griefed by the owner himself. I wanted 
to fix the griefing issues so that the other players wouldn’t suffer from the lack of rule 
enforcement. The server owner, however, was an obstacle to any good changes. To create a 
system that adapted to the practical application of the rules, I resorted to inciting outrage within 
the playerbase to create the pressure for change. I created a court system that claimed to keep the 
powers that the owner and I held in check, but its true purpose was to give me the ability to 
categorize between violations such as the differences in severity that griefing can have. 
The admin team created to help us ended up being filled with people only slightly more 
competent than the owner, who was the only one who could appoint new admins. They were 
rarely involved in any actual moderation and were essentially just regular players with a fancy 
title. There was this one problem player who held the favor of the owner, allowing him to wreak 
havoc on the server. No other player had ever pushed my capacity to enforce the rules that the 
owner himself wrote. He found ways to bypass anti-griefing systems and had the owner 
constantly argue in his favor whenever I tried to ban him. It didn’t help that the owner’s control 
over the Discord gave him the ability to constantly ping me while demanding to be unbanned. It 
was a textbook example of server mismanagement. I had been looking for a way to leverage my 
power without provoking the owner, and I found it when the Initiator, whom I shall refer to as 
“Player G,” joined the server.
There was no question on whether Player G could be classified as an Initiator, for her 
ambition shined at a level that was impossible to ignore. Her first interactions on the server 
involved ideas for a complete overhaul of the members in administration. Seeing this, I spoke 
with her, hoping her bold methods would encourage more action from the owner. Little did I 
know that this would snowball into a conspiracy to take all power within the server. We had 
discussed the owner’s passivity on the problematic nature of their favored player. She revealed 
that the player had been misogynistic, and it was concluded that we needed to mobilize the 
playerbase to confront and riot against the owner.
title: Running a coup d'etat: a look at the means

content:
Player G was able to use her social media presence to create advertisements which 
attracted about 20 new members. Since the old playerbase had been inactive, she used the loud 
minority to demand better management and express rage over the problem player. The owner, 
panicking as expected, gave her admin permission in the hopes that she would only make the 
minimal amount of changes needed to meet her demands. Knowing that the owner would not 
dare to undo this change, she escalated the situation to create chaos within the server. 
Accusations, mostly of misogyny, were thrown against the admin team regardless of evidence. 
Even the older playerbase, slowly becoming aware of the situation, saw the opportunity for 
change to be more important than whether or not the things being said were true. Only the more 
intelligent players attempted to give the claims any scrutiny. Luckily, those players became 
frustrated with the situation and eventually left the server, removing themselves from being 
potential threats to our new regime. This, of course, was my cue to “negotiate” with Player G for 
the admin team — which I would eventually purge entirely. It eventually resulted in me 
obtaining ownership status of the Discord server, marking our plans as successful and 
completing the coup. 
Hundreds of days of interacting with the owner and administration had given me the 
insight into their strengths and weaknesses. I knew that the owner wouldn’t resist against the 
riots, and negotiated accordingly to strip him of his power. The psychological warfare tactics 
used to bombard the server chats will serve as proof to me of the power of the keyboard when 
wielded in mass. My experiences with Player G will make her a prime example of an Initiator, 
and I will study the exact traits that allowed for all this to happen. In the end, I decided to test a 
combination of two systems focusing on player interaction that I had been slowly developing 
over time. This test may serve as the basis of my theories, providing insight and methods to the 
larger Minecraft server community. This story shall serve to me as an example of how systems 
can be violently collapsed, and how power can be usurped.

Harlow 1 
The Reactionary Nature of Popular 
Answers to the Two Week Phase  
Harlow — June 7, 2026 
IMSC: S-HW-1 
Preface 
 
In the title and throughout this essay, I use the word “reactionary”. This term is typically 
used in politics and philosophy to refer to right-wing ideologies and their tendency to, well, 
react—however, here I am applying it to Minecraft Theory (MT). How I define “reactionary" 
within the domain of MT is different; I define it as follows: describing non-systematic surface 
level analyses of Minecraft that suggest that the problems encountered in Minecraft today are a 
result of changes to the game and its community, and proposing a return to a previous state 
before prior to the changes as a solution to these problems. This term should be considered 
separate but analogous to the common real-world definition. This essay is not here to identify the 
politics of the creators of these videos or people with similar ideas, nor is it here to suggest that 
the ideas posited by these creators are wholly reactionary or even wholly incorrect. What I am 
here to do though is to share a perspective on these videos that has plagued me for quite some 
time. And in turn, I hope to provide a helpful guide on what one should avoid when writing MT.   
 
 
Over the years, as all things do, the Minecraft game and its community have changed. 
What used to be a lesser-known title has become one of the best-selling games worldwide. With 
this has come a very active player base, one which grows a culture of its own, and a studio that 
wants to keep that player base happy. This change has led to many reactions, and more recently, 
criticisms primarily of how the game is played today have developed. My first impressions of the 
game came around 2015 when I played Minecraft for the first time on version 1.8. I remember 
how much I enjoyed it. It was a new world in which my creativity could run wild. I look back at 
it very fondly; a time before I fell into the dreaded loop of the “Two Week Minecraft Phase”. 
However, I recognize that those memories are varnished with childhood nostalgia. I understand
title: The Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase

content:
Harlow 2 
that I will not be able to go back to that time, and thus, I choose to look forward to a new 
Minecraft experience—one that adapts to the context of today, using Minecraft Theory. The same 
cannot be said for many of the popular solutions proposed online around the time the Two Week 
Minecraft Phase was being popularized. Mostly on YouTube, these videos have garnered a lot of 
popularity but not much critique despite the fact that they don’t adhere much to our ‘modern’ 
understanding of these topics and are actively reductive in their analysis. This popular view can 
be illustrated by the videos that will be analyzed here, which are: SirGiovanni’s video, “How To 
Make The 2 Week Minecraft Phase Last Forever”, with over 100,000 views and over 500 
comments and niko’s video, “The 2 Week Minecraft Phase Explained”, with over two million 
views and over five thousand comments. The early ideas presented in these videos should be 
considered reactionary within the realm of Minecraft Theory. 
 
Reactionary ideas would not develop in a world without problems. Without conflict there 
is nothing to react to. What these popular videos identify as the sources of these problems shows 
us how limited their frameworks are. They present a world in which change spontaneously 
appears and starts to cause problems—niko’s video highlights this quite nicely. His general 
analysis advocates playing the game “without subscribing to whatever the current update or meta 
is for the game right now” (2024, 6:30). While there’s nothing wrong with viewing certain ways 
of playing the game as detrimental, niko doesn’t identify this, he is specifically talking about 
what is “new”. Without explaining what the problem with the new update or meta is; niko 
focuses on the appearance of a problem in the symbol of change without getting to the 
underlying problem with the change. Another problem he addresses is that content creators don’t 
play the game how it is “meant to be played” (niko, 2024). In his argument, he suggests that 
content creators who seek popularity and profit are fostering a community in which Minecraft is 
played in the wrong way, and therefore playing the way a YouTuber plays is what is hurting your 
Minecraft experience; rather than any sort of structure that incentivizes this behavior.  
Slightly different in presentation, SirGiovanni posits a functionally identical analysis. 
SirGiovanni’s argument is different in that it focuses more on what has been “lost” than what has 
been gained (not in a positive way) from change. A prime example of this is how he believes 
creativity has been “lost” within the Minecraft community (2024, 5:13). This analysis is surface 
level. It doesn’t present any cause-and-effect behind it, and as a result of this, he does not give a
title: The Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase

content:
Harlow 3 
remedy beyond, “be more creative”. Earlier in the video, he discusses a similar sense of loss, 
saying that “we’ve gotten away from expanding worlds and playing on worlds long term” 
(SirGiovanni, 2024, 3:12). Similarly to the point on creativity, the creator characterizes a change 
as bad without making a case for it. SirGiovanni’s way of thinking exemplifies the non-
systematic element of reactionary MT. His line of argumentation is functionally analogous to 
niko’s because of how it implies that the past was better without identifying any underlying 
problems—but simply saying that it is something to be returned to. The creators identify an 
issue, but they fail to show how the issue arises. Why do you think that it is only now that 
YouTube affects how the game is played? Why is there a loss in creativity now? These are 
questions that a reactionary analysis of Minecraft cannot answer.  
 
So, what is the aforementioned past that they advocate we should return to? Rather than 
actually looking into the past, they’re referring to what they prescribe as the correct way of 
playing Minecraft. They don’t bring up how Minecraft was designed nor how it was intended to 
be played according to the developers, but they declare how Minecraft is meant to be played and 
how it should be played. What they use as evidence is an appeal to intention, constituting an 
intentional fallacy (see: Britannica, 2016). In niko’s video, he provides a seemingly relatable 
anecdote to his viewers; saying, “we all have that one friend who speedruns the game to the point 
to where he has 64 Diamond Blocks and 43 Elytras…Minecraft was not meant to be played like 
that; It was meant to be played at a much slower pace” (2024, 3:37). He presents a problem 
which, as he says, “we all have”, and then he juxtaposes it with what he interprets as the 
“correct” way of playing the game. This creates a binary understanding of how Minecraft is 
played, simplifying it to a point unrecognizable from reality. Also, small side tangent, this 
framing, particularly in using the word “speedrun”, serves to devalue speedrunners’ work and 
enjoyment of the game. People who speedrun are not “enjoying the game in the wrong way” 
because there is no wrong way to enjoy a game. Speaking from personal experience, game 
designers try to encourage certain behavior or feeling in their design, however this does not mean 
that players will actually adhere to the designers’ intention, nor does it mean that the designers’ 
intention is the most fun way to play a game—at least not for everyone. A similarly simplified 
idea is presented by SirGiovanni, claiming that “in the newer versions we just get so caught up in 
doing all the extracurricular things… that we kind of forget the core reason why we play this
title: The Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase

content:
Harlow 4 
game and why this game was made in the first place” (SirGiovanni, 2024, 2:21). Once again, we 
see an appeal to intention, as well as a somewhat obscured appeal to nature in implying the 
existence of a core reason for playing the game that we all have (see: Britannica, 2012). Both 
niko and SirGiovanni go on to basically say that building and what they call “creativity” are the 
intended ways of playing Minecraft (niko, 2024; SirGiovanni, 2024). We see them develop this 
argument with something generally considered positive, which is creativity, and saying that that 
is what Minecraft is about. These ideas are reactionary in that they revert back to a simplistic 
model of Minecraft in order to justify their view of intention and nature being the superior way 
of playing the game. The problem with these reactionary ideas is that they present a “correct” 
way of playing Minecraft, which is a highly black and white view and directly antithetical to the 
common understanding within the contemporary Minecraft Theory community. 
 
Now that we understand their arguments, we can look at what they have to back it up, 
which is… nothing. As alluded to previously, neither of the videos here actually cite anything. 
Their entire understanding and basis of their thesis is anecdotal evidence that they presume you, 
the viewer, have experienced too. Not even an example to point to, it’s purely based on vibes and 
rationalizing themselves into a world view. They don’t even pretend to understand Maslow’s 
hierarchy of needs! This is fine, of course, within the context of a YouTube video; people don’t 
go in expecting a source of authority. They weren’t made in the context of MT—it is only now 
that the subject is taken a bit more seriously within a small, albeit passionate niche. Even a lot of 
MT YouTubers don’t cite their sources (though, references to other videos may be made). It 
becomes a problem once they do start presenting themselves as a source of authority without 
qualifying that their ideas are purely their own without any evidence beyond anecdote. All of this 
is to make a very obvious point; these videos should not be taken seriously within the realm of 
MT. Other than understanding the development of MT, they are redundant and reductive in 
understanding Minecraft as it is. How they present their argument is not the direction the MT 
community should go in; something that MT YouTube especially should keep in mind. If we 
want to be taken seriously, we first need to take ourselves seriously and in doing that recognize 
when and when not to lend credit to something. 
 
Something in particular that we should not take seriously is when these videos use 
emotion over evidence. SirGiovanni and niko employ the use of nostalgia to resonate with their
title: The Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase

content:
Harlow 5 
viewers. This goes hand in hand with the ideas presented that Minecraft just used to be better, 
referring to the game and the community. An example we see throughout both niko and 
SirGiovanni’s videos is the use of older versions as background visuals (niko, 2024; SirGiovanni, 
2024). The use of these visuals serves as a trigger of childhood nostalgia within the viewer. This 
then forms the association between their argument, their prescription, and that feeling. The 
assumption that, in the cloud of nostalgia, they were playing the game in the “correct way” in the 
past, according to SirGiovanni and niko’s assessment. Nostalgia isn’t a concept that they are 
trying to hide from the viewer, of course, both of them freely bring up how nostalgia plays a role 
in the desire to play Minecraft (niko, 2024; SirGiovanni, 2024). However, they don’t go further 
beyond this, they don’t investigate whether this emotion is clouding their judgement. This is a 
reactionary position—viewing the past through an idealized lens as a source of authority on the 
matters of today. This doesn’t mean that nostalgia should never be discussed within MT circles, 
but nostalgia should never be used in the place of real evidence. 
 
SirGiovanni, niko and anyone else positing similar ideas are not acting in malice or trying 
to mislead. These videos came out before the IMS, before the currency debate, and before 
anything else we would consider Minecraft Theory, but they show a clear desire to understand 
the game that they love. When analyzing a piece of media, it is easy to get caught up in the 
sentimentality of things. Presenting Minecraft as a misunderstood masterpiece is a romantic idea, 
an infantilizing one. But that ideal can lead to reactionary tendencies. These reactionary 
tendencies then lead to actually misunderstanding Minecraft on a fundamental level. I wouldn’t 
even say that all the ideas that they present are wrong per se, I agree that playing Minecraft at a 
slower pace will lead to more enjoyment, I agree that social media has played a part in making 
the modern Minecraft experience worse, and I agree that creativity is important. However, the 
difference is that I see change as an avenue for solutions rather than a malicious force that should 
be avoided at all costs. Minecraft Theory should be considered a science, and science is based on 
evidence, proper analysis, and the scientific method. In that way, science and reactionary thought 
are inherently contradictory. If we, as Minecraft Theorists and as members of the IMS, want to 
foster a community that is healthy, taken seriously, and respects evidence and the scientific 
method, it is necessary that we understand that the reactionary approach to Minecraft analysis is 
actively detrimental and counter-productive toward our goals as a community.
title: The Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase

Preface 
While I was writing this essay, Turtle approached me and asked me to take over the 
operation of the Systems Experiment. I accepted, as I want to see the IMS and this event 
succeed. This is, of course, a potential conflict of interest, but I chose to disclose this 
information here because it is relevant to the context of this critique. For this reason, I also 
ask that you scrutinize this essay under that context. Though, I will not alter the language or 
any of my critiques in the essay to accommodate this change. Will I implement any 
significant measures in the event to offset the problems I bring up? Probably not. I’ll try to 
communicate more to the best of my ability, but at this point in the event, it would be actively 
counterproductive and would also go against what I argue for. However, I welcome and will 
encourage people to criticize how I then run it. 
Minecraft Server Theory arguably began with someone who actually put their theory 
into practice. PineconeLP’s “Raid Farms” has been discussed at length in the IMS, whether in 
passing or as the focus of an entire essay or video—there’s no doubt that it's influential. 
However, having only one example of a server using MST in its design becomes quite 
problematic in the long term for the field. As a result of this, there’s a large amount of people 
in the IMS who’ve expressed wanting to experiment more, thereby putting more ideas into 
practice. This is difficult, of course, because running a server takes a lot of time and money, 
time and money that people don’t have. And that’s not even taking into account whether or 
not people want to run control studies or get studies peer-reviewed. For this reason, there
title: The Consequences of Poor Design: A Critique of the Systems Experiment

content:
Harlow 2
have not been many experiments. 
The Systems Experiment is an event run by Turtle (turtle2770), an administrator at the 
IMS, who set out to create a space to run experiments. Unfortunately, the event fails at this 
goal. What could’ve been an environment, where members of the IMS could test their 
systems, was not. This essay is a look into what exactly went wrong and an urge to do right 
in the future. In writing this critique, I acknowledge that Turtle has a lot on his plate at the 
moment, and I sympathize with him as someone who often plans events myself. This is not a 
criticism directed at Turtle or any of the other organizers of the event; I have immense 
respect for their efforts. The Systems Experiment is an example of a well-intentioned, 
however, very flawed attempt at experimental research—flaws caused by its lack of adequate 
communication, ad hoc decision making, and lack of scientific integrity. 
Effective communication is the foundation of any good event, and really any sort of 
social activity. Communication can make or break the success of an event. And it’s 
unfortunately one of the biggest flaws of the Systems Experiment. Outlining well-defined 
goals is a prerequisite for effective communication. While the goals of the event were 
described in the Manual and Handbook, most people seemingly hadn’t read them; indicated 
by the lack of a common sentiment held by the participants and certainly not one that most 
people understood. According to the Manual, the goal of the event was to make an 
environment fit for people to create and test systems in a vanilla setting while offering a 
competitive aspect (“Full Manual”). The lack of a clear goal in the eyes of the participants is 
indicative of the inadequate communication by event organizers, which then leads to a 
disconnect between the participants and organizers, hurting the overall event experience. 
Along with this, there were scenarios during the event where the lack of 
communication from event organizers actively hurt my own team’s “systems.” This mostly 
revolved around the mechanics of the event, mods, rules, etc. One of my teammates' systems 
heavily relied on the number of Nether portals allowed per team. We received unclear 
communication on this issue so much so that it was contradictory at times. The changes to 
certain mechanics were often hidden behind a thread on the suggestion or question board. An 
example of this is how my team, Ordonia, wasn’t aware of the wiretaps mod, while team 
Alpha was. Moreover, there were mods that neither team was made aware of. Inadequate 
communication hurts the results of the experiment, both in that inconsistent knowledge leads 
to inconsistent participants, i.e. uncontrolled participants, and in that it makes it hard for 
people that are trying to learn from the event to understand the parameters and context of the
title: The Consequences of Poor Design: A Critique of the Systems Experiment

content:
Harlow 3
Systems Experiment. 
The lack of communication, however, is a symptom of another problem. Since the 
inception of the event, it has undergone many changes. It’s not certain how many were due to 
participants' suggestions and how many were merely the result of an organizer’s change in 
mind, but both of these avenues played a role. These changes were a misstep in the running of 
the event—they were often impromptu and unplanned while also being counterproductive to 
the goals of the experiment. To be clear, this is not coming from the angle of, “all change is 
bad.” A lot of the changes made by Turtle were good, and as I’ve outlined in my essay, “The 
Reactionary Nature of Popular Answers to the Two Week Phase,” anyone who adopts such 
an approach is mistaken. However, in this essay, we will consider the changes from the 
perspective of experiment design as well as participant experience where we find that they 
are counterproductive in achieving the goals of the experiment. 
While ad hoc decision making may sound like not the worst thing, or perhaps, it may 
even sound positive—what’s wrong with adaptability after all? For an experiment, it can be 
extremely detrimental. Changes introduce new variables into the equation, variables that 
weren’t in existence before. These new variables render any data in between the changes to 
be in different contexts. Assumptions made with previous data must be reevaluated in a new 
context. This ad hoc decision making is further fueled by the “Suggestions” board on the 
Systems Experiment Discord server. Allowing players to have an input is usually a good 
thing. It allows players to build what they want to play and deepens a sense of community. 
However, in an experiment allowing participants to significantly affect the experiment 
creates some problems. For one, obvious reason: It affects the outcome of the study, 
precluding scientific testing of a hypothesis. Even if your participants are running their own 
“studies,” these changes affect everyone, not just the participants who want the change. Not 
to mention that players are participants in their own experiments, which is opening up a 
whole other can of worms we will get to later. For these reasons, on the spot decisions just 
don’t work if you want to yield reliable results. 
On the player side of things, changes can foil any plans participants try to make. 
Especially in an event like this where planning is the name of the game, unpredictable 
changes can introduce problems that simply cannot be prepared for. Bringing us back to the 
Nether portal example. The rule was debated frequently, not only by participants but by 
organizers as well. The decision was only finalized nearly a week into the event. This meant a 
week of uncertainty on whether my teammates' system would actually work. The uncertainty

Harlow 4
surely has knock-on effects (i.e., frustration and burnout), resulting in the loss of players the 
event desperately needs. These effects are antithetical to the goals of the event.
The frequent, ad hoc changes seen above suggest a lack of foresight and planning in 
the design of the Systems Experiment. It’s understandable to want to meet the needs of the 
players, however, it comes at the cost of procedural control, a price that cannot be afforded in 
a situation like this. In that way, the Systems Experiment is sacrificing its ability to offer 
reliable results, compromising by pandering to participants’ own sensibilities. Ironically, 
these ad hoc choices also made participant experience worse; creating an environment where 
it’s hard to plan or even enjoy the event at all. 
While the name of the event is the Systems Experiment, Turtle has stated that it is not 
an “experiment,” and it was named the way it was for “branding” purposes (turtle2770. 
2026A, 2026b). Even if we suppose that its goal is to allow people to experiment with new 
systems, it blunders. You’ll frequently come across decisions that seem counterintuitive to 
achieving Systems Experiment’s goals. In the “Design Mission” section of the manual, it 
states that one of the event’s goals is to create systems that could “realistically be used by 
players in almost any server” (“Full Manual,” 1). This suggests a desire to be able to 
generalize the results of experiments to areas outside of the “lab” (turtle2770. 2026c). While 
this goal is stated, it is not seriously taken into consideration. 
One of the most glaring of these problems is having the designers of the systems be 
participants in their own experiments. It should be pretty obvious why this is a bad idea. The 
designers of the systems design them the way they do because they think it may work, 
hoping for it to succeed. This is clearly a conflict of interest. Consciously or not, the system’s 
designers will affect the outcome of the system in ways that would not otherwise be seen. 
There are scenarios in research where you may want to have a researcher “participate” but 
only as a perceived peer by other participants which can be controlled (this kind of researcher 
is called a “confederate”). 
 Further problems are found within the very nature of the event itself. The event, 
being a competition, encourages using and sticking with systems that might otherwise be 
faulty in the name of winning a competition. It creates a scenario where the players have an 
investment in keeping systems alive beyond their efficacy and material benefits. While this 
may represent some servers, it certainly does not represent most. It also discourages 
potentially malicious or otherwise self-interested players from interacting with a system in a 
way that is unexpected (i.e., a loophole). Even if such players are annoying, they are
title: The Consequences of Poor Design: A Critique of the Systems Experiment

content:
Harlow 5
extremely important to understanding a natural server’s environment. 
Not only does the Systems Experiment present a conflict of interest in how it is 
structured. This kind of attitude toward non-invested players is enshrined explicitly into the 
rules of the experiment. Later in the manual, it describes the rules of the event, one of them 
being that “a player is not allowed to try to purposefully evade the mechanics of a system,” 
(“Full Manual," 10). A page below this rule, on allowing people to go without designing a 
system, states, “while it sounds fine in theory, this will introduce a lot of members who want 
to focus specifically on SMP style play. They are likely to get annoyed with systems over 
time and bypass them,” (“Full Manual,” 10). These rules may be well-intentioned, however, 
like with the structure of the event, they introduce a biased sample and a skewed dataset 
towards systems-oriented players. These rules are diametrically opposed to the goal of 
creating systems that could “realistically be used,” (“Full Manual” 1). 
Another sampling bias we see is due to the large amount of IMS members who joined 
the event. IMS members are interested in server design, and as a result of participants 
primarily being interested in server design, they consciously decide not to engage with certain 
features they deemed incompatible with the goals of the server. One of my teammates 
proposed that we went without using one of the mods used by the server entirely. This does 
not reflect natural player behavior that is necessary in experimentation; the average player is 
far more interested in achieving their own goals than in adhering to an idealistic purism based 
on a niche online community. This problem could be waved off as a failure in advertising. 
However, it connects to the issue of not allowing non-systems-oriented players into the event 
as well. The barring of non-design interested players from participating, whether indirectly or 
not, is detrimental to the usefulness of the data and therefore detrimental to experimentation. 
Despite it being the foundational goal of the Systems Experiment, the event wasn’t 
able to offer a testing ground that yielded generalizable conclusions. Thus, the “experiment” 
has failed to progress the field of MST. This is demonstrated by the biased effects that come 
from designers participating in their own systems, the nature of competition, and the 
exclusionary rules and invitations into the event. It’s an example of a lack of scientific 
integrity which should be learned from for the future. 
In this critique, we’ve seen a contradiction between the goal of a fun gamified 
competition (i.e. a good event) and allowing participants to test their own systems in a 
controlled environment (i.e. a good experiment). This contradiction ends up hurting both 
goals in the end. The event struggled to communicate with participants effectively while
title: The Consequences of Poor Design: A Critique of the Systems Experiment

content:
Harlow 6
trying to listen to as much as possible. Decisions were made in the moment, hurting the 
research value of the experiment, while claiming the goal of creating a space for 
experimentation. Furthermore, the design itself discouraged reliable and generalizable results 
that can be applied to many different servers. Don’t take this as a call to change the Systems 
Experiment. As I’ve explained above, that would likely hurt the experiment even more. Let 
the Systems Experiment, my and hopefully others’ critiques of it, be a learning experience 
for the IMS in its forthcoming scientific endeavors. Let it pave a new path forward for 
Minecraft Server Theory.

Staff responses to political discussion have caused the  chilling effect to appear

law, rule, or action has a chilling effect, it tends to discourage discussion, limit 
freedom, or cause some other harm.” This effect leads to self-censorship, as people 
fear potential repercussions.
As an example, in June 2026, IMS members were discussing buying an online 
domain for the Institute. One member jokingly suggested using a .gov domain, to

Wild or Mild? The Wilderness Bound 
Update
By Llamangus
 IMSC: S-LS-2
What the Wilderness Bound Drop adds
The Wilderness Bound Update is quite large for a seasonal drop, seeing as we have a new 
biome with unique trees and foliage, new structures, updated explorer maps, new stairs and 
slabs, and a cushion. This is the largest drop released in a while. By placing features into 
different buckets we can see what they bring to the table and what they add to the trends 
within Minecraft updates. 
The Dappled Forest brings Poplar and a pop of autumn for builders and 
terraformers.
The Dappled Forest brings a decent amount of content that gives more leverage to builders, 
terraformers, and for world-painters and custom biome developers. The red ground foliage is a 
nice addition next to regular and dried grass and bush blocks. Youtuber Kanokarob has quickly 
put these to use to create a ‘winter biome update’ 1 creating a new ‘thawed’ tundra biome. The 
autumnal colors of the foliage fits in well for a muddy alpine valley or boggy arctic lowland. The 
drops system is almost perfect for these small bonuses that the Minecraft community can 
creatively leverage into various aesthetics or systems. 
The Biome itself fits an interesting niche, with bold reds, bright colors, and dark muted waters to 
provide a backdrop for moody or scenic builds. New England covered bridges, to agrarian 
settlements celebrating a harvest festival, rugged hunting lodges, or stoic northern castles – the 
Dappled Forest is probably uniquely situated in its potential among the ‘weird’ biomes in that it 
carries with it varied but specific real-world associations. 
Weirdness Explained
The ‘Weird’ part is actually a parameter that Minecraft uses to generate biomes alongside 
Temperature, Humidity, Continentalness, Erosion, and Depth. ‘Weirdness’ is… well, a weird 
1Kanokarob. October 2026. “UPDATING Minecraft’s Snowy Biomes”. https://www.youtube.com/watch?
v=6Gvc6ZatW0Q
title: Wild or Mild? The Wilderness Bound Update

content:
name for a parameter, but it performs multiple duties alongside the other parameters. Weirdness 
can help determine, for example, if a forest should be a regular forest or flower forest, and if a 
jungle should actually be a bamboo jungle. 2 Weirdness operates on a scale between -4 to 4, 
and some biomes generate within either positive or negative weirdness. ‘Peaks and Valleys’ is 
downstream of Weirdness, which helps to determine the elevation of terrain. These forests 
often generate under the conditions of Moderately Cold Temperature, Very Low Humidity, and 
High Weirdness. 3 They seem to spawn near plains biomes due to this, as opposed to near other 
forests. There are currently no variations of the dappled forest as of yet, similar to the Cherry 
Grove. A variety of Dappled Forest type biomes could make a region of them seem larger, 
similar to Birch Forests, Savannahs, and Jungles. 
Tiny Dappled Forests
Dappled Forests can generate in a large range of sizes, but comically small dappled forests 
became a topic of discussion. With weirdness topped onto the temperature and humidity 
requirements, these are not common biomes. 
Seed hunters sought progressively smaller Dappled Forest Biomes, with youtuber Petchiy 
finding one that is as small as a one-by-one!4
The Verdict
So is the Dappled forest Mild or Wild? Let’s recap. 
-
Builders and Terraformers Friend: I’ll give it eight Zombie Horses out of ten. It’s 
legitimately different from the rest of the offerings aside from the greyish poplar wood 
fitting in the same lighter spectrum of wood types alongside birch and pale oak. Though 
it still earns its keep as a wood type apart from those. 
-
To the biome itself, I’ll give it seven TNT minecarts out of ten. It’s quite a pretty biome, 
and meaningfully fits a niche that hasn’t been represented previously.
Averaged Verdict: 7.5
Roads? Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.
Many of you have likely started a new world or server, only to bee-line to the nearest village, 
and take it over to build your very own big-box store with unpaid interns. You probably also 
built your base there, and somewhere in your chest rests your 19th saddle which you definitely

Well guess what? The villagers still can’t tell you to spend some time away from the comforts of 
their village, but this update adds a few new things that will probably exist under most peoples 
radars in due time, but hear me out.
Group together the straw beds, the new explorer maps, and the abandoned campsites, and you 
get a pretty nice package deal that goes particularly well with the previous ‘Bundles of Bravery’ 
update. 
Given what we know about biomes, there’s quite a lot of them, and searching for one in 
particular might be quite the task. That being said, this might be the start of a different way to 
play the game. With weird biomes, weirder caves, and yet weirder dimensions, perhaps 
temporary shelters, maps, and different modes of travel will be the way of the future for some.
The Publishing Departments Editor in Chief has made a point in the past about biome

almost a necessity for this. 
We’ve yet to see what Mojang has planned for Minecraft's other dimensions, should they have

of Ten. Aside from straw beds, they’re likely to be overlooked, but they are there, silently

be enough to save themselves from you. They’ve seen your automatic chicken farm. 
But in all honesty, these features might not be big on their own, just as it was once easy to 
overlook the bundles. These are the features that will matter over time, in the aggregate of 
additional features, biomes, and dimensions. But still, perhaps the camps are a bit like an 
advertisement of the possible. A good horse or mule, some organized and colored bundles, 
wool slabs and stairs, fences, campfires, and workbenches, and maybe a spyglass. What more 
does a person need past that but the sunset or the sea? The content is somewhat mild, but the

context could be wild.
A Cushy Situation
Three wool slabs (another object released this drop), or one and a half wool blocks and you’re 
about to do something that plugins, datapacks, and build hacks have been used to do for years. 
You get to sit. Not only do you get a seat, but an entity that can be placed at a sub-block height, 
and remain there so long as it’s on a block's hitbox.
The intended use case of the cushion is big on its own, because you have a dyeable, deployable 
entity to sit on that isn't bulky or designed to move. 
Already there are catalogues of furniture designs. 
But the unintended uses for the cushion are also quite big. Cushion based transportation 
methods make for rapid bridge crossing, and cushions can be used to get to the nether roof or 
surface of the overworld. Redstoners have used cushions to create colorful displays with copper 
bulbs and redstone lamps under cushions. 
Still, the casual utility for decoration, for accessing the nether roof, for social gatherings, and as 
a prop for content creators, means it’s a very versatile feature sure to be found in a player’s 
inventory as much as any niche tool is. 
The Verdict:
Honestly, Nine Zoglins out of Ten, very wild. 
Honorable mentions. 
These two features could be bundled up with the previous ratings, as Straw Beds fit in the same 
theme as the maps and abandoned camps. Wool stairs also generate as tents in the camps, and 
are beloved furniture pieces. However, they stand out on their own and thus deserve 
honorable mentions. 
1. Straw Beds: Useful, but somewhat expensive for a one time use. They could be a hassle 
to replace if used in builds, if you accidentally enter them. Functionally this could have 
been a sleeping bag that didn’t break. Four hungry sheep out of Ten. 
2. Wool and Concrete Slabs and Stairs. These could be separated on their own, as concrete 
is a more niche and harder to obtain block. Wool stairs and slabs have a much broader 
set of use cases in furniture, tents, and roofs. It’s difficult to assign a numbered rating 
for this, but wool is a stronger case over concrete, and we are still missing terracotta 
stairs and slabs. It’s earned a respectable seven out of ten.

With scores ranging between 5.5 to 9, and an average total score of 7.25, we can safely say this 
update is fairly wild. 
A seven might seem low, but for a drop it’s fairly solid. It’s part of a pattern of drops that seems 
to hint to where Mojang wants the game to go. More exploration and exploration tools, 
without leaving the builders and the technical minecrafters empty handed. These drops tend to 
focus on less dramatic but highly leverage-able features that build up over time. 
As for what this means for Minecraft Theory and Minecraft Servers? It’s hard to say what this 
means definitively for the field, or what we can expect for sure, but we can look at the trends:
1) The addition of maps seems like a genuine solution to a problem of scale within the 
overworld. If more unique ‘weird’ and/or ‘single’ biomes are added, we could expect 
perhaps more biome specificity, more reasons to explore, gather, and trade. Perhaps an 
early game ‘green’ market for renewable goods, and maps to biomes, will develop. 
2) Cushions fill a genuine void, while affording a small amount of personalization with dye 
colors. Players can sit without needing anything but stable, deployable cushions. 
3) Abandoned camps seem like a small thing, but they serve a purpose for finding more 
structures and biomes, and they may be an advertisement for a less settled type of 
gameplay. 
In conclusion, it seems fair to be optimistic about where the drops system might continue to 
take us, especially as we look into the future towards The Sift, which still leaves us with more

the most part, been solid. Even when they don’t change the survival meta on their own, they 
open up a range of playstyles and building choices for players.

What The Sift tells us about Dimensions
By Llamangus
IMSC: S-LS-3
Aspirational Adventures
Minecraft Live, 2026: Lady Agnes saw us off with the following statement: “The Sift is one 
important step on our Aspirational Adventures Journey. But, it is not the end of it.”
This hurried statement struck a chord with many that have been wanting an end update.1 We’ll be 
waiting longer for that, but that’s probably for the best. 
The Sift feels like a fresh, colorful start for the Minecraft of today, as they’ve turned a simple 
indie block game into something expansive. The Sift belongs to this moment, this decade, in 
ways that the Nether and End don’t. 
Many players avoid the challenges of the Nether and the End, but perhaps The Sift can offer 
enough new opportunities to break that pattern. New wood types to fill the rest of the 16 color 
range, new stones, new pets for companions or zoos, new material alternatives to Netherite2, and 
new opportunities to expand in ways that Minecraft hasn’t yet. 
What players and developers can learn from The Sift and Aspirational Adventures may be 
takeaways that they need in order to bring the spirit of the new into the old. It’s not the end yet 
for Minecraft.
New Mobs, a New Groove
Historically, base mobs were introduced quite slowly into the game. Varieties off of base forms 
are a safe bet, but The Sift is positively vibrant. New passive and hostile wildlife are bound to be 
present from what we’ve seen in Dungeons 2. It remains to be seen what niches will exist in base 
Minecraft. 
Minecraft Dungeons 2 also provides more bosses, and more lore to the Illagers. It’s too early to 
assume there will be a direct translation, but perhaps The Sift will provide us new bosses and

is=zAMAkBEIdA8mk5iC
2 Minecraft. April 2021. “Ask Mojang #16: Tools and Gear”. https://youtu.be/ndDttLXhAeE?is=1lS6j5c5H6szeylN

content:
new difficulties without the fear of fire and lava or the void that has kept casual players in the 
overworld. 
Ichor: Nutritious Nectar or Torpid Terror?
It’s not quite lava or water, but a mythical substance found in The Sift. In Dungeons 2, it inflicts 
soulsickness, draining players of health and souls. 3
There are no ‘souls’ mechanics in base Minecraft presently. There is room for speculation about 
the loss of experience as the overworld sculk releases experience. Experience storage is possible 
for mob farms using a sculk catalyst. 
Almost certainly, Ichor will have a technical use, but if The Sift has the ‘healthy’ version of 
Skulk and wardens, what does that mean for Ichor transported into other dimensions? Could it 
behave differently in the overworld? 
Conclusion
The Sift presents more questions than answers at this point. The adventures may be aspirational, 
but I suspect the biggest aspiration might be changing how players think about progression. The 
End is flawed, and rushing to get the Elytra can break the game. The End isn’t what it could be, 
but a new approach on developing the middle and end game may be what the cleric called for. 
Perhaps The Sift is another beginning for an aspirational reimagining.

Summer event announced with ongoing votes deciding server 
components 
IMSC: S-MA-2 
Background 
As the Institute of Minecraft Studies expands, the organisation has begun work on planning 
its first in-game event. The first-of-its-kind event is set to be held during the summer months, 
when most members are expected to be able to attend. 
The experiment’s democratic, member-led planning stage was officially launched by Turtle 
on 15 April 2026, a senior member of the IMS and head of the Department of Synthesis. The 
upcoming event is also supported by KingGame2000, who has obtained access to a server for 
a short period. The senior figures also worked together to establish the aim of the summer 
event. 
It was announced that “…each player would choose and operate a specific system within a 
single Minecraft survival server,” indicating that players will be able to control aspects of a 
Minecraft society to mimic a real-life civilisation. These types of “civ events” have long been 
popular in the Minecraft YouTube space; however Turtle clarified that there would be 
“[interactions] with the systems that their team creates to test them and create real dynamics.” 
The novel project will aim to simulate the real world as closely as possible to provide insight 
into how Minecraft players behave in the sandbox game, whereas most civ events are 
optimised for YouTube viewership. This distorts the real experiences and conflicts players in-
game may have, as a system of conformity is created through the setting of the server. The 
organisation also further emphasises the real and human aspect of the event, allowing and 
encouraging players to act freely and with their own will. 
This unique set-up will also allow some empirical data to be taken, which may advance some

Planning to “include you all” in the decision-making 
The chief organiser has also expressed his desire to “include you all” in the decision making

New member-created logo for the IMS announced 
IMSC: S-MA-3 
After the name change of the IMS (from MSTI) on 17 March, co-ordinated and initiated by 
Turtle, submissions for a new logo opened. Previously the organisation used a block render of 
a server created by u/pietromarcucci on r/Minecraft, which was directly nipped off that post. 
Nevertheless, the IMS now needed to create its own identity and establish its own self. As in 
any transition, after you change your name, you may also elect to change your appearance. 
Further clarification and guidance was released a few days after about the contents of a logo 
submission, emphasising its need to be “recognisable” and be able to “attach meaning”. 
And so submissions began flowing in, and on 19 April, ten logos were able to be voted on. 
Design 1.8 by scorevon won in the end with 18 votes of 99 ballots. This result is obviously 
far from democratic and proportional, but ultimately the logo received positive praise and 
recognition. After some refining and creating the design in Minecraft, the IMS logo was set: 
an inverted cube with a command book at the centre, with a gray/green colour palette. 
I had a few questions, so I contacted the artist, who very kindly gave me a few minutes of his 
time. Most logos and brand designs are expected to be appealing and stick to your memory, 
but IMS is not a “brand” per se. When asked why such a usually dull and unflashy colour 
scheme was chosen, scorevon explained that “…the grey scheme creates a more cohesive and 
refined appearance.” Any design must consider its context, and this logo took into account 
the IMS’ professional and theory-oriented purpose. The organisation does not chase 
popularity (although it is important to spread our ideas), but instead scientific rigor where 
possible, deep analysis, and establishment of theories. 
Further, like how banks are made of marble acnd granite to symbolise stability, the balanced, 
stoic, and firm atmosphere of a gray logo showed to outsiders the IMS’ dedication to help 
members, and others, to “…create these systems better for their worlds.” The green sector, 
for me, ties everything back to Minecraft. That the institution is not a “wishy-washy fun 
police” that attempts to academicise the sandbox game, but to seek to improve the playing 
experience that many servers (and singleplayer worlds!) lack. 
Any change can either be for the better or worse, and I believe this will be a new slate for the 
IMS. Being one of the more veteran and senior members of the IMS, I always had a wish for 
the organisation to be a popular alternative interpretation of what it means to have fun in 
Minecraft. We are (probably) the first people to establish such a community, and to have it 
grow to over 200 members is a sign of our popularity. 
With this new logo and colour theme, we can make promotional material ahead of the 
Systems Experiment in the Summer, and the new banners and logos have already been 
applied to the IMS website. 
Finally, I asked the last, but very important question: “What made you join the IMS?” 
The creator told me he wanted to “…learn from other members, contribute meaningfully to 
the community, and play an active role in developing defensive systems in Minecraft.”
title: New member-created logo for the IMS announced

content:
And my face began to grin. The space I now have such a huge role in contributing to is meant 
exactly for this — co-operation, learning, and creating. For such a long time we have seen 
servers rise and fall, promising great community and absolute freedom, hoping that players 
will bind together eventually. You cannot have a server that automatically makes people 
interact, co-operate, and build infrastructure without engineering it to do so. Our institute is 
now the home of these discussions and debates, and for this, I am intensely proud. 
Moreover, the designer said they wanted “…[to have] political systems in Minecraft servers.” 
This is also another one of my personal goals in the IMS, where politics can be tested and 
tried with real players and people, all the while gathering data and creating theses to explain 
their behaviours. Having published the First Edition of the IMS Journal alongside my 
colleagues, we have already laid the groundwork for this kind of theory creation and a space 
where different ideas can be heard and given wide recognition. 
For now, the IMS will remain to be a small group of enthusiasts. However, with the Systems 
Event coming up, and some exciting promotional material I have been told is coming up, I 
have no doubt at all we will grow. We will become the home of debate and discussion on 
Minecraft Theory, just you wait.
title: New member-created logo for the IMS announced
